POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Thu, 01 Oct 2026 21:35:48 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.9 Israel’s Herzog calls British sanctions a ‘grave mistake,’ accuses UK of election interference https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/01/israels-herzog-british-sanctions-criticism-01104187?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 01 Oct 2026 21:32:53 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9096701 Israeli President Isaac Herzog accused Britain of intervening in his country’s elections through sanctions he called “unfair and politically motivated,” urging his European allies to talk with Israel before blaming the country.

“I was very disturbed and offended on behalf of my nation regarding the sanctions that were laid against us by the U.K. government,” Herzog said Thursday in an interview with Axel Springer Global Reporter Network’s Jan Philipp Burgard. “I think it was a grave mistake.”

Earlier this month, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced that Britain, along with France and Canada, would ban the trade of goods and some services originating from Israeli settlements. Miliband also said the U.K. would take action against companies and individuals providing services for settlement expansion.

Miliband then said that the British government agreed that Palestinians were facing “ethnic cleansing” in parts of the West Bank, adding that “all too often the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this.”

Herzog rejected the approach, arguing it would worsen the situation rather than help Palestinians.

“It’s directly intervening in Israeli politics, which shouldn’t have happened,” he said. “You want to move things, have a dialogue with Israel and don’t blame Israel.”

The dispute comes ahead of Israel’s October elections, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu seeking another term as Israel faces growing international isolation.

“And I ask all my friends in Europe and all the other nations, please do not intervene in our elections,” Herzog added.

Israel previously responded to the announcement by saying it will retaliate by closing the British consulate in Jerusalem and warning of possible “countermeasures” against other countries.

]]> en Albania’s PM to US Democrats: Don’t use us to get revenge on Trump https://www.politico.eu/article/albania-edi-rama-democrats-revenge-donald-trump/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 01 Oct 2026 19:08:36 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9095459 TIRANA, Albania — Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama took a playful shot at U.S. Democrats over ongoing “Flamingo Revolution” protests against a planned luxury resort backed by Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law.

What started as protests against the project has evolved into broader anti-government protests and is now entering its 124th consecutive day, drawing widespread international media attention.

Rama attributed this attention to the “long shadow of Donald Trump,” in an interview with WELT, which, like POLITICO, is part of Axel Springer’s Global Reporters Network.

He added: “I told my Democratic friends in America: If you cannot beat Trump in America, do not come to Albania to take revenge. That is not fair.”

Kushner is linked to a multi-billion-dollar project to develop a luxury resort on the uninhabited southern Albanian island of Sazan and an adjacent strip of shoreline next to a protected area inhabited by flamingos, pelicans and diverse wetland wildlife. The plans sparked national and international protests at the end of May, with rallies ongoing every night outside Rama’s office in Tirana.

The protests drew widespread attention, with a resolution in the European Parliament, and international clothing brand Patagonia, and Kosovo-Albanian pop singer Dua Lipa getting involved.

Rama said the plans involve two projects: One on the publicly owned Sazan Island, a former Soviet military base, with only 8% to be developed, and another on a privately owned peninsula.

Protestors object to the project over environmental concerns and a lack of public consultation. Meanwhile, the country’s EU- and U.S.-backed Special Prosecutor’s Office for Organized Crime and Corruption, SPAK, is investigating whether an Albanian businessman faked ownership documents related to the private land.

The former owner has denied any wrongdoing. A spokesperson for the project’s investors, including Kushner, did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication.

Objecting to protest slogans such as “Albania is not for sale” and “Albania for Albanians”, Rama said, “If you were bringing foreign capital into Germany, would you then say that Germany was being sold off?”

“I represent the interests of my country, and I will continue to do so,” he added.

He also said negotiations over the project were still ongoing and that they would assess its environmental impact.

At a press conference in Tirana Wednesday with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Rama assured that his government will “shine a spotlight on the process by ensuring full transparency regarding all documents related to this widely discussed project.”

While Rama met the EU Commission chief, several hundred people protested outside his office with placards reading “No EU with Rama.”

]]> en As Germany’s far right rises, weakened Merz looks to project strength and resolve against Putin https://www.politico.eu/article/germany-far-right-friedrich-merz-project-strength-resolve-against-vladimir-putin/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 01 Oct 2026 18:48:14 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9095249 BERLIN — German Chancellor Friedrich Merz moved to reassure allies in Europe and Kyiv that his domestic political weakness would not erode his government’s support for Ukraine as the war nears its fifth winter.

The chancellor also sought to convince an increasingly wavering German electorate that it is in their direct interest for Berlin to provide military support for Ukraine — warning that failure to remain united behind Kyiv could one day invite a Russian military attack on Germany.

“If we fail to rein in Moscow, the Russian war machine will, sooner or later, turn against us and against NATO,” Merz said during a speech at a ceremony in the western German city of Münster, where the alliance was awarded the Westphalian Peace Prize. “We must not turn a blind eye to this danger. Three generations after 1945, war would return to our part of Europe.”

Merz went on to warn of the danger of conflict in Europe with some of his most dramatic language yet.

“Would the Baltic states then become a battlefield for drone warfare, just as Donbas is today?” he said. “Which major European cities would be targeted by the ballistic missiles that Russia is currently firing at the populations of Kyiv and Kharkiv?”

“Would we Germans ultimately be targeted as well? Would we once again experience the horrors of war firsthand? Ladies and gentlemen, our most urgent European and transatlantic responsibility today is to do everything in our power to avert this.”

Merz’s comments came weeks after the far-right Alternative for Germany party recorded its best-ever election results, coming in first in two regional votes in the former East Germany, while the chancellor’s conservative Christian Democratic Union suffered historic defeats. The conservatives’ poor results were widely blamed on the deeply unpopular chancellor, prompting internal debate within his own party over whether to replace him.

The surge in popularity for the Kremlin-friendly AfD sparked concerns in Kyiv and across Europe that Germany — which under Merz has become Ukraine’s greatest military supporter — could falter in its support for Ukraine. The AfD — a party that favors ending military support for Ukraine and re-establishing economic and energy ties with Moscow — is the most popular party in the country, according to surveys, polling well above Merz’s conservatives.

Merz on Thursday took aim at the AfD, portraying the party as a conduit for Moscow’s influence and vowing that his government would continue to support Ukraine despite hybrid attacks and disinformation campaigns “orchestrated from Moscow” and spread through “the slogans of the AfD and its Russian backers.”

At the event in Münster, Hendrik Wüst — the premier of North Rhine-Westphalia and the conservative politician often held up as a possible replacement for Merz — praised the chancellor’s leadership in what appeared to be an effort to project unity and quell talk of a so-called “chancellor swap.”

“Chancellor Friedrich Merz assumed a pivotal role in NATO during a critical phase,” Wüst said ahead of Merz’s speech, commending the chancellor’s “clear commitment” to NATO’s 5% defense spending target. “While others hesitated, the German chancellor stayed the course, thereby providing stability to the alliance,” he went on, adding: “Thanks to you, dear Friedrich, it is clear that Germany is making a strong contribution to peace and freedom.”

While Merz and Wüst sought to project stability and resolve to an international audience, many of the chancellor’s remarks aimed to convince an increasingly wavering German electorate to stay the course on military support for Ukraine.

Many Germans continue to express worry about a potential Russian attack on NATO territory. According to a recent survey for German public television, 42% of respondents said military support for Ukraine goes too far — the highest proportion yet. Opposition to military support for Ukraine is particularly prevalent in the former East Germany, where the AfD is strongest.

“Ukraine must get through this winter, and I am convinced it will. It can count on our help,” Merz said.

“If we falter in Germany, then Europe falters,” he added. “If we remain steadfast, then Europe will remain steadfast.”

]]> en EU ministers explore new emergency migration measures https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-ministers-new-emergency-migration-measures-ceuta-spain-morocco/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 01 Oct 2026 18:31:15 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9095051 The mass influx of migrants into Ceuta over the summer has placed a controversial migration measure on EU ministers’ agenda.

In July, the sudden arrival of more than 70,000 migrants to the small Spanish North African territory triggered chaos, just as the EU was rolling out sweeping migration reforms to secure its external borders. Several countries argue that it should be possible to temporarily suspend asylum applications in crises of this scale under a new emergency procedure.

“If 70,000 people — mostly young men— arrive in a single day, then that obviously has nothing to do with asylum,” Austria’s Interior Minister Gerhard Karner said Thursday. “And if that’s the case, then the existing regulations aren’t sufficient to handle it.”

Earlier this week, Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner presented plans to prevent and address sudden mass arrivals on the bloc’s borders that may be engineered and weaponized by other countries, including a ramped-up role for border agency Frontex.

The blueprint also included a European emergency response framework, which Commission President Ursula von der Leyen had included in her State of the Union address last month.

“We need to be able to react quickly to such emergencies when they come about,” Brunner said Thursday. He added that EU leaders would continue discussions at a meeting later this month, and that the Commission would make a proposal “on that basis.”

With talks Thursday not yet focused on specific proposals for the European emergency response framework, several countries were in wait-and-see mode.

Athens has proposed temporarily suspending asylum applications in emergency situations, and the German and Austrian ministers have signaled support for the idea.

Diplomats and ministers from three other countries said they’d wait for the Commission’s proposal before taking a position. Diplomats also raised concerns about the impact of suspending asylum applications — which could effectively result in large-scale pushbacks banned under international law — on fundamental rights, but agreed the EU needed to discuss it.

“There is obviously a tension between the right to asylum and 80,000 people appearing at the border of, for example, Ceuta,” one EU diplomat, granted anonymity to discuss the private talks, said ahead of Thursday’s ministerial. The EU also needs to discuss “what can and cannot be done” in an emergency without violating people’s rights, the diplomat said. “It’s a hard nut to crack.”

“The need for having these kinds of emergency tools is pretty clear to us. The discussion is whether it should be on the EU level or more on the national level,” Sweden’s Migration Minister Johan Forssell said.

“If there would be an EU mechanism, it’s crucial that [it] won’t constitute a problem” for countries like Finland and Poland, which already have protective measures in place, he said. “Otherwise there’s no use having an EU response.” 

The discussion moves the debate around EU migration policy in a new direction that’s bound to cause controversy, just as ministers adopted another controversial reform that allows member countries to send failed asylum-seekers to deportation hubs in countries outside the bloc.

Civil society groups have criticized the so-called return hubs as “legal black holes,” but a group made up of Austria, Germany, Denmark, Italy and Greece is meeting regularly to lay the groundwork for such centers.

Spain was the only country to vote against the reform; Belgium abstained. Ireland and Denmark have an opt-out to EU justice matters and didn’t participate in the vote.

]]> en British-Iranian man arrested in RAF Fairford investigation https://www.politico.eu/article/british-iranian-man-arrest-raf-fairford-investigation/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 01 Oct 2026 17:59:47 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9095318 LONDON — U.K. counter-terrorism police have arrested a British-Iranian man on suspicion of terrorism offenses as part of their investigation into an incident at RAF Fairford.

The 25-year-old was arrested in London on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts under Section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006. (Police initially misstated his age.)

Police also said a second man, 26 and a U.K. national, has been questioned under caution, and officers have searched two properties as part of the investigation.

Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing Vicki Evans said: “The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of inquiry.”

“As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles – including possible foreign state involvement. I’d like to thank the public for their continued support and patience whilst we work through this investigation.”

Five U.K. nationals from London were detained on Sep. 27 after receiving a report of suspicious vehicles near RAF Fairford, which is used by the U.S. Air Force.

They were arrested on suspicion of offenses under the Explosives Act and later, preparation of a terrorist act. They have since been bailed but remain under investigation.

On Wednesday, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC that Britain believes Iran “to have played a part” in the incident.

Earlier this year Britain gave permission for the U.S. Air Force to use RAF Fairford to carry out “defensive” strikes against Iran. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has previously warned the U.K. that British military bases used by the U.S. to launch strikes would be a “legitimate target.”

This article has been updated.

]]> en Un budget “réversible” ? Ce que le prochain gouvernement pourra vraiment défaire https://www.politico.eu/article/un-budget-reversible-ce-que-le-prochain-gouvernement-pourra-vraiment-defaire/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 01 Oct 2026 17:43:23 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9094847 PARIS — Réversible, adjectif : “qui peut revenir en arrière, qui peut se produire en sens inverse”, selon le dictionnaire. Alors que s’ouvre le long chemin budgétaire, préparez-vous à entendre cette définition répétée à l’envi par le gouvernement.

Lors de la présentation jeudi des projets de loi de finances et de financement de la Sécurité sociale, obtenus par POLITICO (ici et là), les quatre ministres David Amiel, Roland Lescure, Stéphanie Rist et Jean-Pierre Farandou, ainsi que leurs cabinets ont maintes fois insisté sur le fait que les textes financiers sont conçus pour pouvoir être défaits rapidement après l’élection présidentielle.

“C’est une liberté inédite que nous souhaitons laisser à nos successeurs, quels qu’ils soient”, a appuyé David Amiel, le ministre des Comptes publics.

Le gouvernement met cet argument au cœur de son travail de conviction auprès des oppositions — en particulier du Rassemblement national — pour qu’elles ne fassent pas barrage au budget.

Le mode d’emploi

Parmi les mesures modifiables, celles de gel sont les plus faciles à rectifier. A commencer par la disposition qui pourrait être la plus urticante du budget de la Sécurité sociale : la désindexation des pensions de retraite au-delà d’un seuil fixé à 1 260 euros par mois, soit 4 milliards d’euros d’économies espérées.

Comme l’a révélé POLITICO, le mécanisme astucieux — “atypique” dans les mots du cabinet de David Amiel — propose un dispositif à trois étages permettant de revaloriser en dessous de l’inflation ou de geler les pensions par décret.

Celui-ci pourra être pris jusqu’au 31 octobre 2027 et s’appliquer rétroactivement au 1er janvier. Une sorte de clause de sauvegarde qui permet de laisser le choix au prochain exécutif, après la présidentielle, de revenir sur un gel total ou partiel.

“Ça me rend dingue, on prend une décision nécessaire et courageuse sur les retraites, et on donne la possibilité à Marine Le Pen de revenir dessus dès le premier jour”, s’étrangle un député EPR auprès de POLITICO, qui regrette que l’on dépossède le Parlement pour tenter d’éviter la censure.

Même logique pour le gel des APL, de la prime d’activité, du seuil des allègements généraux des cotisations sociales ou encore du point d’indice des fonctionnaires. “Tous les gels sont réversibles, a insisté David Amiel. Le futur gouvernement pourra revenir dessus dès sa première semaine aux affaires.”

Cet argument ne convainc pourtant pas Eric Coquerel. Pour le président de la commission des Finances et député LFI, si le gouvernement voulait réellement éviter de figer les choix budgétaires avant la présidentielle, il aurait pu opter pour une loi spéciale (soit la reconduction provisoire du budget précédent) et laisser le prochain pouvoir arbitrer.

La nécessité d’un budget bis

Cette “souplesse” mise en avant par le gouvernement présente toutefois des limites pour les grandes mesures fiscales. Contrairement aux gels ou aux mesures explicitement conçues pour pouvoir être modifiées par décret, les principales dispositions fiscales du PLF comme du PLFSS ne pourront être supprimées ou modifiées que par une loi de finances rectificative.

En leur temps, Nicolas Sarkozy ou François Hollande ont utilisé cette possibilité dès l’été de leur arrivée au pouvoir, pour tenir rapidement quelques promesses en matière d’impôts. En 2017, le gouvernement d’Edouard Philippe, lui, avait préféré opter pour un décret d’avance afin de sabrer dans les dépenses de l’Etat et de dégager 4,5 milliards d’euros d’économies, dans le but de ramener le déficit public sous la barre des 3% du PIB.

Sur le front des dépenses, la réversibilité ne se décrète pas non plus d’un trait de plume. Les crédits ministériels peuvent être annulés ou réorientés en cours d’année par décret, mais seulement dans une certaine limite.

Toute augmentation au bénéfice d’un autre ministère suppose de trouver des économies ailleurs. Et au-delà d’un certain seuil — environ 12 milliards d’euros dans le budget de l’Etat —, il faut là encore repasser par une loi de finances rectificative.

Pour des engagements symboliques, comme les chantiers immobiliers gérés par l’Etat, actuellement suspendus pour les moins urgents, nous expose le cabinet de David Amiel, les travaux pourront reprendre à la demande du nouvel exécutif.

“La réalité, c’est qu’il y a une énorme forme d’inertie sur le budget, une fois même qu’on a commencé à l’exécuter, un nouvel exécutif aura plutôt tendance à se concentrer sur la préparation du budget suivant”, analyse un artisan de l’élaboration du budget, qui juge par ailleurs la communication “plutôt habile”.

“C’est du bon marketing et un magnifique exercice de style, avec un recours accru marqué à des renvois réglementaires pour plein de trucs et des entrées en vigueur différées”, commente un ancien de Bercy.

Reste que l’argument de la réversibilité ne tient… que si le budget est adopté.

Comme l’a résumé mercredi le ministre des Relations avec le Parlement, Laurent Panifous, devant l’Association des journalistes parlementaires (AJP) : “Ce que nous souhaitons, c’est mettre de la souplesse, mais d’abord que cette souplesse soit validée par le Parlement actuel.”

Judith Chetrit a contribué à cet article.

]]> fr EU, Ukraine agree to accelerate €45B loan payout in 2027 https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-ukraine-agree-to-accelerate-e45b-loan-payout-in-2027/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:46:39 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9092738 BRUSSELS — The European Commission and Ukraine have reached a deal to accelerate the disbursement of €45 billion earmarked for Kyiv in 2027 under the EU’s €90 billion loan program, they said Thursday in a joint statement.

Russia has in recent weeks escalated its drone and missile attacks against Ukraine, while the country is running out of funds to buy weapons to defend itself.

Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi warned journalists this week that Ukraine faces a $27 billion (€23 billion) defense funding gap this year, with Kyiv hoping to cover about $7 billion domestically and looking to partners for the rest. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that if the gap isn’t plugged in the next two months, Kyiv risks being unable to buy weapons early next year.

At a recent meeting of EU defense ministers, “many called for front-loading parts of the €90 billion loan allocated for 2027,” meaning disbursing part of the 2027 loan this year instead, the EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas said last month.

But the Commission preferred to instead speed up the disbursement of the 2027 loan next year itself, meaning Ukraine would get that money faster, diplomats said.

“Our dialogue with the European Commission has delivered good results in addressing Ukraine’s financial and defense needs for 2026 and 2027,” Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. “We have agreed on the format, timeline, and steps needed to ensure full coverage,” he added.

“For 2027, we have agreed to move forward swiftly with the allocation of €45 billion under the Ukraine Support Loan, subject to the established conditions,” the two sides said, referring to the reforms Ukraine must carry out to receive the money. Once Ukraine meets the conditions, the funds will be immediately disbursed, according to a senior EU official.

The two sides also agreed that they will “begin work on identifying additional budgetary and defence needs” and meet monthly to coordinate their efforts.

The €90 billion EU loan was agreed by leaders last December to provide financial support to Ukraine in 2026 and 2027. It includes strict conditions for Kyiv, including adherence to the rule of law and the fight against corruption. A large share of the loan — €60 billion — is earmarked for Ukraine’s defense needs.

The loan has been split evenly, with €45 billion earmarked for 2026 and another €45 billion for 2027. It was designed to cover two-thirds of Ukraine’s external financing needs over the two years, with the rest expected to be covered by other countries, particularly G7 partners.

The joint statement also calls on those partners to step in.

“All sides agreed that other partners should also fulfil their financial commitments and step up their efforts in light of the significant challenges Ukraine is facing,” it says.

Zoya Sheftalovich contributed to this report.

]]> en ‘We have not delivered’: Germany’s Wadephul criticizes slow EU enlargement progress https://www.politico.eu/article/germanys-wadephul-criticizes-slow-enlargement-progress/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 01 Oct 2026 16:01:26 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9093278 BUDVA, Montenegro — German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul urged EU countries on Thursday to deliver on enlargement promises to the Western Balkans, warning that the bloc’s credibility and its influence in the region are at stake.

“We are at a crossroads with the EU enlargement process,” Wadephul told reporters following a meeting in Montenegro held as part of the Berlin Process — in which EU and Western Balkan countries discuss economic integration and infrastructure in the region as well as reconciliation among the Balkan countries.

Wadephul argued that the EU had declared the Western Balkans belonged in the bloc at a summit in Thessaloniki in 2003. He added, in a critical assessment of Germany’s own efforts, that former Chancellor Angela Merkel launched the Berlin Process 11 years later, in 2014, to speed up the process, but that another 12 years later and there was still no success.

“We have not delivered,” the minister said, adding: “I would really urge everybody to show them that the promise of Thessaloniki was real, that we are credible, that Europe is reliable.”

Wadephul also referred to “geopolitical adversaries and rivals” vying with the EU for influence in the region — a thinly veiled reference to Russia and China. On Wednesday, Republika Srpska Prime Minister Savo Minić and his predecessor Milorad Dodik visited Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, ahead of elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina on Sunday.

Austria’s foreign minister issued a similar warning: The EU must “understand that the clock is ticking. And the clock is ticking very quickly on a global scale. We can no longer afford to get bogged down in bureaucratic — and, until now, technocratic —processes,” Beate Meinl-Reisinger told POLITICO in an interview.

“If we give any leeway — even just a millimeter — other foreign powers will be here in a flash and will take advantage of it,” she said.

Montenegro is on the frontline of EU enlargement, aiming to become the bloc’s 28th member in 2028. EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos has praised the reform efforts of the country, saying that 18 of the 33 EU accession chapters had already been closed and that “several more” were expected to follow this month.

“There is a realistic chance that Montenegro will conclude negotiations by the end of the year or early next year,” she said, even though ratification would then take another one to two years.

Montenegro’s Foreign Affairs Minister Ervin Ibrahimović told reporters that his government had undertaken many reforms, adding that his citizens must now also be able to reap the benefits of EU membership.

“To be honest, we deserve to be admitted now,” Ibrahimović said.

]]> en ‘Thank you, Andy’: Farage gloats as Burnham reopens Brexit fight https://www.politico.eu/article/thank-you-andy-farage-gloats-andy-burnham-reopens-brexit-fight/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 01 Oct 2026 15:52:26 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9093680 LONDON — Nigel Farage told Andy Burnham to “bring it on” if he wants to fight a general election on rejoining the European Union.

The Reform UK leader, a veteran Brexiteer, claimed in a speech on Thursday that the British prime minister has given him the “biggest boost in my career” by reopening the EU debate.

Burnham used his first conference address as Labour leader this week to open up the possibility of Britain trying to rejoin the bloc it left after the 2016 referendum.

Polling has suggested a shift in public support towards rejoining the EU since then — but it remains a deeply divisive issue in U.K. politics. 

Farage claimed that Burnham will be “in for a shock” — and tried out his arguments against trying to rejoin the bloc.

Those include a claimed £25 billion annual price tag for re-entry, a wave of immigration under freedom of movement, and a claim that Britain would be forced to join the Euro.

Each of these will doubtless be disputed by the government if Burnham does choose rejoining as one of several options he’s floated for a reboot of European ties after a general election.

But it shows the attack lines that Farage would relish fighting a campaign on. 

“It’s just so contradictory,” the Reform UK boss told supporters at Doncaster racecourse.

“He says he wants to unite the country,” Farage said of Burnham. “A second referendum will divide the country bitterly in a way perhaps we’ve never seen before.

“If Andy Burnham — the ‘King of the North’ — wants a fight in Doncaster and the Red Wall with me on rejoining the European Union, then bring it on, I say.”

The choice of Doncaster for the speech was no coincidence. The northern city strongly voted to leave the EU, and lies in the so-called “Red Wall” that was once Labour’s industrial heartlands.

“He might have just given me the biggest boost in my career I’ve ever had. Thank you, Andy,” Farage added.

Return to campaigning

The Reform leader used the speech to kick off a promised stretch of constant campaigning.

Farage acknowledged he had been “relatively absent” from the limelight during a summer in which his party has been dogged by questions over the probity of donations to Reform.

He launched what he dubbed a “100 Days to Save Britain Tour” — billing it as the start of Reform’s general election campaign.

“And I will be out on the road every week between now and the general election, whether it happens this year or next spring or in three years’ time, we are back out actively campaigning and fighting,” Farage said.

A spokesperson for the Reform leader promised he’d be making stops on this tour “at least twice a week” up until the election — barring holiday periods. 

Farage still believes an election will be called as early as the spring, but it’s in Burnham’s power to call one as late as August 2029, and the prime minister has spent the past few days publicly damping down expectation of one.

]]> en Diesel américain : la France et quatre autres pays européens s’accordent sur une réponse “ferme” https://www.politico.eu/article/diesel-americain-la-france-et-quatre-autres-pays-europeens-saccordent-sur-une-reponse-ferme/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 01 Oct 2026 15:50:05 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9093488 BRUXELLES — Cinq pays européens, dont la France, ont convenu lors d’une réunion d’urgence jeudi de répondre “d’une seule voix” aux pressions croissantes exercées par le gouvernement américain pour qu’ils libèrent leurs réserves stratégiques de gazole, a appris POLITICO auprès de plusieurs personnes au fait des discussions.

La France, l’Allemagne, la Grande-Bretagne, l’Italie, l’Irlande et la Commission européenne ont pris part aux discussions visant à déterminer comment réagir face aux pressions exercées par l’administration Trump pour qu’ils réduisent leurs stocks de pétrole, sous peine de voir les exportations américaines de gazole interdites, ont relaté trois responsables européens à POLITICO.

Tous ces pays ont subi des pressions en coulisses de la part des Etats-Unis pour qu’ils réduisent leurs stocks de pétrole, sous peine de se voir imposer un embargo sur les exportations américaines de gazole, ont indiqué deux de ces responsables.

Ces pays, ainsi que l’exécutif européen, se sont mis d’accord sur trois points, selon ces mêmes interlocuteurs : réagir à la pression d’une “voix coordonnée”, veiller à ce que “toute décision concernant la libération des stocks soit portée au niveau de l’AIE [l’Agence internationale de l’énergie]”, et s’efforcer d’“apaiser les tensions dans les échanges avec les Etats-Unis”.

L’AIE, dont le siège est à Paris, coordonne la politique énergétique des pays développés et a supervisé le déblocage de stocks pétroliers en début d’année, à la suite de la fermeture du détroit d’Ormuz.

L’idée, c’est de “désamorcer” la situation, a expliqué l’une des sources mentionnées plus haut. “Il s’agit d’adopter une attitude à la fois ferme et positive dans la communication […] Quand on a affaire à un lion affamé, on ne lui joue pas forcément des mauvais coups.”

Un groupe plus large de pays, dont certains ont également subi des pressions de la part de l’administration Trump, se réunira vendredi pour discuter de la réponse à apporter, a ajouté cette source.

POLITICO avait précédemment rapporté que le secrétaire américain à l’Energie, Chris Wright, avait mis sur la table une alternative : plutôt qu’un embargo sur les exportations de diesel — dont dépend fortement l’UE —, il demandait que des stocks stratégiques de pétrole soient mis sur le marché.

Les prix du diesel s’envolent aux Etats-Unis en raison des guerres en Ukraine et en Iran. Et la pression s’accentue sur Donald Trump pour qu’il fasse baisser les prix à l’approche des élections de mi-mandat, qui s’annoncent décisives.

Il n’est pas question pour le président américain d’exclure une interdiction des exportations, malgré la forte opposition du secteur pétrolier américain. “J’y réfléchis”, a déclaré Donald Trump lors d’un événement à la Maison-Blanche. Après avoir assuré en parler régulièrement avec d’autres membres de l’administration, il a déclaré que ceux-ci “pensent, en quelque sorte, que cela aiderait le diesel, mais que ça pourrait faire augmenter le prix d’autres produits”.

Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Alexandre Léchenet.

From Rome to Budapest, governments have been rolling back the progress, with initiatives stalling all the way up to EU level. ]]> Europeans have lead the field on access to abortion, but a conservative comeback has caused a lot of those advances to regress.

Research published earlier this week (28 September) by the Centre for Reproductive Rights (CRR) found that despite an upward trend of legalisation, some countries are still seeking to enforce barriers and rolling back entitlement to abortion care.

This resistance to change is also evidenced in the lack of member state participation in safe abortion funds available since the the ‘My Voice, My Choice’ European citizens’ initiative for safe and accessible abortion was passed into law last February. 

EU funds could since then be used to create regional programmes for safe abortion care for anyone who can’t access it in their own country, as well as financing travel to a country where abortion is available.

However, no funds have yet been used.

]]> [Interview] Le Pen and Mélenchon are ‘economically illiterate’ and weaponising migration, says French scholar ahead of 2027 race https://euobserver.com/238893/interview-le-pen-and-melenchon-are-economically-illiterate-and-weaponising-migration-says-french-scholar-ahead-of-2027-race/ Thu, 01 Oct 2026 13:20:43 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=238893 French political scientist Jacques Rupnik says the economic illiteracy of Marine Le Pen and Mélenchon is astonishing. He anticipates that in the first round of France's presidential election, most voters will back a candidate they believe can stop Le Pen. A Mamdani moment could happen, since people feel that politics has exhausted itself.]]> “Marine Le Pen has reinvented herself. Her style now is more moderate,” reckons Jacques Rupnik, a French political scientist, ahead of the country’s widely anticipated battle for the presidency.

Many voters in France will vote for the candidate they see as having the best chance of defeating the far-right leader, Rupnik explains.

“All polls show that if the far-left Jean-Luc Mélenchon faced Marine Le Pen in the second round of France’s presidential election, Marine Le Pen would win,” he says, explaining that many French votes are unwilling to back Mélenchon.

In his interview with Denník N, Rupnik claims Mélenchon is the first French presidential candidate to seek support from immigrants so explicitly.

Find out:

  • How Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon have used the migration debate for their campaigns.
  • Why the presidential frontrunners do not understand economic issues.
  • Rupnik’s assessment of Emmanuel Macron’s two presidential terms.
  • Who does Marine Le Pen look up to?

Polls suggest that if France held a presidential election now, far-right Marine Le Pen and far-left Mélenchon would make the second round. What does this tell us about France?

France is divided and polarised. Young people in particular tend to lean towards more radical parties. Establishment parties are old and worn; they have lost their appeal. They have little to say, except for claiming that others are dangerous or worse. But you must bring something new to an election. But after ten years of Macron, that is very difficult.

And it is not entirely true that all polls predict Mélenchon will reach the second round; they often place former prime minister Edouard Philippe ahead of him. Mélenchon is powering ahead in polls because he has launched his campaign and is very good at it. But, nothing is decided.

In French presidential elections there are two rounds. In the first round, you vote for your preferred candidate; in the second, you vote for the lesser evil. So, for most voters, the question will not only be whom they prefer, but also who has the best chance of defeating Le Pen in the second round.

And that is very important. All polls say that if Mélenchon faced Le Pen in the second round, he would lose. Many people are not willing to vote for Mélenchon. A centrist candidate has the best chance of defeating Le Pen, so for now it looks like former prime minister Philippe.

But only if another former prime minister, Gabriel Attal, withdraws his candidacy.

Yes. We have two strong parties at the extremes, and the space in the centre has shrunk. The narrower it becomes, the more candidates appear within it. Every week, another politician tells media: “You know what, I would give it a go.”

Attal, of course, wants to win over Macron supporters — that is, voters on the centre left. The fact he is in the race matters even if he withdraws and endorses another candidate. That may prove a good strategy.

Read more

Can new French PM ‘Baby Macron’ help beat Le Pen?

If Le Pen and Mélenchon reach the second round, many would vote Le Pen. Why?

Marine Le Pen has reinvented herself. Not in the sense that she has been thinking about what new ideas to bring forward, but now her style now is more moderate. It is no longer the brash style associated with her father.

Perhaps she took her cue from Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni, seeing a candidate whom everyone feared, but no radical changes followed her election because she adapted quickly to European realities.

Le Pen points out that in several European countries, including Finland and Sweden, the far right has been in government and nothing has happened.

At the same time, Marine Le Pen managed to break through a certain barrier, and some moderate rightwing voters have shifted to her side.

Read more

Le Pen and Farage – the far-right always play the ‘victim’ card

How did that happen?

Previously, the moderate right was stronger and Le Pen’s camp was weaker. The type of rightwing voters who voted for Jacques Chirac have now shifted their weigh behind more radical options. The balance has shifted, and right-wing voters are saying: “Why should we, the right, be excluded from politics simply because Macron has failed and the Le Pen has grown stronger?”

Immigration is another reason behind growing support for Le Pen. Mélenchon is also capitalising on the immigration debate, but in the opposite way to her.

Please explain that.

Mélenchon opposes Le Pen’s position by arguing that immigrants integrate. The Le Pen camp says: “No, they have come from a different culture and their attitude is anti-French.” Le Pen’s camp says that integration works poorly, that immigrants do not even want to integrate instead preferring to live in their own communities.

“Mélenchon has therefore adopted the theory of grand remplacement, but instead of presenting it as a threat, he has turned it into a huge opportunity.”

And Mélenchon argues that it is fine for immigrants to remain in their own communities, practise their own religions, for women to wear headscarves and so on.

The great replacement conspiracy theory (“grand remplacement“) should be mentioned since the far right embraced it long ago. It is the idea that the native French population will gradually be replaced by new immigrants.

And Mélenchon now says: “What great replacement? On the contrary, it is an opportunity for France. He says: “The more of us there are, the better.”

Mélenchon has therefore adopted the theory of grand remplacement, but instead of presenting it as a threat, he has turned it into a huge opportunity. Of course, everyone knows what he is aiming for. It is an election campaign, and he is appealing to voters who are themselves immigrants.

Previously, no one focused on immigrants in elections except Le Pen who used them as a bogeyman. And now Mélenchon says: “We are appealing to Muslims.” He says Muslim headscarves are fine and religious symbols are fine. He says anyone who opposes this is racist.

In August, Le Pen announced her intention to ban headscarves in public spaces. Will her anti-Islamic agenda help her win?

On the contrary, such statements mainly play into Mélenchon’s hands. Of course, calling a referendum on the issue in France is not so simple since such laws already exist. The law states clearly that you can do what you want at home, but if you work in the public sector you must refrain from displaying your religion. There are laws covering this, and there is absolutely no need to devise new ones. Le Pen’s ideas in this regard seem to be mere campaign slogans; we cannot take them literally.

Read more

Islamic veil can be banned in workplace, says EU court

Yet, a major Le Monde poll shows the French are more concerned about the economy than immigration. Immigration ranks fourth, after social issues and ecology.

That is true, but other polls show that, for many voters, the issues of migration and safety overlap considerably.

So, as concerns about security become increasingly prominent, people are more concerned about security and often link it to migration. Marine Le Pen will certainly try to make it one of the key issues, alongside the economy.

]]> Listen: How does Trump’s AI pact compare with the EU? https://euobserver.com/240706/listen-how-does-trumps-ai-pact-compare-with-the-eu/ Thu, 01 Oct 2026 11:51:49 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240706 Donald Trump is betting on voluntary commitments from AI companies. On Tuesday (29 September), he unveiled a self-regulatory agreement drawn up with some of the biggest names in the AI industry.]]>

Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

Find the full transcript below: 


Donald Trump is betting on voluntary commitments from AI companies. On Tuesday (29 September), he unveiled a self-regulatory agreement drawn up with some of the biggest names in the AI industry.

What does it mean, and how does it differ from the EU’s Code of Practice for general-purpose AI?

On Tuesday, September 29, Trump brought together the CEOs of some of the biggest AI companies. Together, they signed what could be described as a self-regulation pact: a short list of non-binding commitments called the White House Accord on Super Intelligence.

Read more

AI chatbots turn users’ most intimate data into a potential goldmine for advertisers, researchers warn

That’s the other novelty: Trump no longer wants to talk about artificial intelligence, but about “super intelligence”. The term AI apparently has negative connotations.

So, what exactly have these companies committed to? The CEOs of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, SpaceX and Nvidia have pledged to put safeguards in place, quickly detect and fix problems, and have their systems checked by independent auditors.

The principle of voluntary commitments may sound familiar to Europeans: They echo the EU’s Code of Practice for general-purpose AI — which, like the White House agreement, is not legally binding.

So what’s the difference? First of all, OpenAI, Anthropic and Google have also signed the EU code, while Meta, SpaceX and Nvidia have not.

And, more importantly, the EU does have binding rules in place: the AI Act, which is already in force. As part of this regulation, the European Commission developed the Code of Practice to help companies comply with the rules.

You could think of it as a checklist for AI companies, to help them make sure they are complying with the law.

Read more

Let’s not allow AI firms to use fears of future dystopias to distract Europeans from existing problems

Another difference is the sheer volume of recommendations. The document published by Trump is just one page long. The European Code of Practice runs to more than 60 pages and was prepared with the help of dozens of independent experts.

It is also more comprehensive, covering not only safety, but also transparency and copyright. But this raises another question: if both documents are voluntary,  how effective can they actually be?

When the European Code of Practice was published, some civil society organisations criticised it, arguing that voluntary commitments are not enough and that concrete obligations are needed.

Read more

EU states urged to ‘go beyond’ AI Act to protect people from abusive surveillance

There are binding obligations under the AI Act. But they are not as precise as what is in the code of conduct.

Similar criticisms have emerged since the White House agreement was published on Tuesday. And it is worse in the US case, since companies are absolutely not legally bound by the commitments they have made.

The United States has generally been less inclined towards binding regulation of the sector. Trump has argued that rules can hinder the development of companies, and has promoted a national framework that is as minimally restrictive as possible.

The White House document does leave the door open to legislation in the future. It says that, over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into lows or regulations.

But for now, they remain voluntary commitments. If you are interested in this topic, there will be a live event on Tuesday next week about AI and its safeguards, organised by VoxEurope.

 It will be online and you can find all information on Vox Europe website. 

]]> EU accession of Moldova and Ukraine is alternative to Nato, as Russia draws new Iron Curtain in Europe https://euobserver.com/239313/eu-accession-of-moldova-and-ukraine-is-alternative-to-nato-as-russia-draws-new-iron-curtain-in-europe/ Thu, 01 Oct 2026 10:03:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=239313 With Nato doors closed to Ukraine and Russia pushing a new Iron Curtain across the Black Sea, an “urgent” EU expansion toward Kyiv and Chișinău is emerging as Europe’s main tool to defend its eastern flank and preserve its global clout. ]]> “What is remarkable is that Ukraine and Moldova, despite finding themselves in a very tense situation regarding their security, are extremely keen to move closer to the EU and have therefore already begun negotiations and opened the first cluster.”

These are the words of the deputy director of the European Council on foreign relations (ECFR), Vesela Cherneva, and they come just as the official negotiation process for the two countries’ accession to the European Union has begun.

With this, the EU embarked on a truly geopolitical enlargement – driven not only by the pursuit of shared values, a larger market, and stronger common institutions, but also by the need to safeguard the continent’s security in a shifting environment.

Ukraine: a battle-hardened nation’s journey from the post-Soviet world to the EU

According to Cherneva, the EU’s upcoming enlargement is the only way to institutionally anchor Ukraine within a serious and lasting framework, given that the US position has remained clear under both presidents Donald Trump and Joe Biden: Nato enlargement to include Ukraine is not possible.

“Currently, EU membership is the only way to integrate Ukraine’s and Europe’s security systems. This is an entirely different discussion from negotiations on chapters, clusters, sanitary standards and other accession requirements. We are talking about security guarantees, but also about the transfer of military technologies from Ukraine to Europe and, more broadly, about how Ukraine – which currently possesses the strongest and most combat-capable army in Europe – can, while defending Europe, also become part of the European security debate,” Cherneva says.

Ognyan Minchev, political scientist, professor and executive director of the Institute for Regional and International Studies, an independent think-tank in Bulgaria, also believes that Ukraine’s importance is substantial and that the questions surrounding its integration are highly complex.

“Ukraine currently possesses the only genuinely combat-capable army on the European continent. Western European armies have very limited personnel numbers and, until recently, received extremely low levels of funding. The lack of real resources, including weapons, to address the challenges of military security makes Ukraine a more attractive partner,” he says.

Although many experts would point to Ukraine’s contribution to European security as the greatest benefit of its accession to the EU, the country can also contribute to development in other areas. There is undoubtedly great potential for development in the fields of agriculture and farming.

The country has a vast area of cultivated land and is among the world’s leading producers of a number of cereal crops such as wheat, maize, barley, rice, and others. It exports these products to third countries, and membership would increase the EU’s economic influence in these regions.

Ukraine’s accession could also lead to cooperation between different sectors and result in an increase in meat and dairy production as a consequence of increased cereal production.

Beyond agriculture, Ukraine’s pharmaceutical industry could offer the EU an opportunity to reduce its reliance on imports of generic medicines from China and various Asian countries. Thanks to its favourable climate, Ukraine also has great potential for various types of renewable energy.

Deposits of gallium, rutile, graphite, magnesium ores, lithium and other minerals vital to the green transition could contribute to European production and help the EU compete with China.

According to Minchev, integrating Ukraine represents a major challenge because it involves a large country that is institutionally weak, with high levels of corruption, poor economic organisation and significant shortcomings in the functioning of public life.

Read more

What JK Rowling’s Voldemort can teach us about Ukraine war

“Ukraine has been forced to transform itself into an effective fighting machine, but in other respects it remains a post-Soviet society with serious problems in the areas mentioned above. This makes its rapid integration into the EU extremely difficult,” Minchev says.

Moldova: a key piece in Europe’s security architecture continues to struggle under Russia’s shadow

“For Moldova, we can say that it is a small but significant element in the broader domino effect of Black Sea security, which is becoming an increasingly crucial aspect of overall European security. This is because the confrontation between the Kremlin regime and Europe is effectively unfolding along the line of a new Iron Curtain being formed across Ukraine and the Black Sea region,” Minchev says.

According to Cherneva, Moldova’s accession is also crucial precisely because the country is a buffer state, and Russia has demonstrated that it does not tolerate buffers.

Read more

[Interview] Moldova races for EU membership by 2030: ‘We owe this chance to Ukrainians’, minister says

“Russia seeks to conquer and control such buffer zones. If Moldova does not want to share the fate of Belarus or Georgia, it must take rapid steps towards European integration,” Cherneva says.

For years, Moldova has served as a testing ground for Russia’s hybrid warfare. As Western European countries are only now confronting the full scale of Russian hybrid attacks, Moldova has already spent years developing its own resilience and countermeasures.

The country brings to European security valuable expertise gained from combating Russian disinformation and resisting repeated attempts by the Kremlin to interfere in its domestic political processes.

Yet Moldova’s accession would have implications extending far beyond security. Although it possesses far less agricultural land than Ukraine, the country has the potential to make a meaningful contribution to the European agricultural sector. Moldova has been gradually integrating into the EU’s Single Market through the Deep and Comprehensive Free Trade Area (DCFTA).

]]> Europe’s children will inherit public-health crisis from new EU pesticide approvals https://euobserver.com/240266/europes-children-will-inherit-public-health-crisis-from-new-eu-pesticide-approvals/ Thu, 01 Oct 2026 09:37:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240266 By extending pesticide approvals and keeping hazardous products on the market, Brussels is bending to Big Pharma and causing a food-system and public-health burden for decades to come.]]> The European Union once prided itself on leading the world in protecting children. Today, policymakers backed by big polluters are betraying that promise in the name of “competitiveness”. 

In June 2026, Florence, Franck, and Isabelle packed their bags and headed to Brussels. Why? Because their children have all suffered serious harm from pesticides. 

These children have endured physical pain and heavy medical procedures, including repeated chemotherapy treatments. And their families have shouldered both the financial and emotional burdens alongside them.

As Isabelle puts it: “It destroys a family.” Her own daughter has been fighting leukaemia for the last seven years.

And they are not alone. In 2024, almost one in 20 children in the EU were exposed to dangerous levels of pesticides; that’s 380,000 kids. Now these parents have a clear message for policymakers: prioritise public health and stop dismantling the rules that protect children against harmful substances. 

In 2024, around 316,000 tonnes of toxic pesticides were sold in the EU to be sprayed across our countryside, risking not only the health of farmers but also polluting our soil, air and water.  

The European Environment Agency in Copenhagen has reported environmentally unsafe levels of pesticides in about a quarter of Europe’s rivers. In groundwater – which supplies 65 percent of the water we drink in Europe – unsafe levels were detected in 11-18 percent of water bodies. 

In the same year, trifluoroacetic acid, a harmful “forever chemical” that forms when ‘PFAS’ pesticides and F-gases break down, showed up in 94 percent of drinking water samples tested across 11 EU countries. 

We are surrounded by pesticide pollution. It’s even in our homes. 

But what’s happening in Brussels?

In December 2025, the European Commission proposed a legislative package that would remove fundamental environmental and health protections against pesticides in the EU.

Among other changes, the proposal – ironically labelled the ‘Food and Feed Safety’ Omnibus – suggests extending pesticide approvals indefinitely and relaxing the rules to allow pesticides already identified as hazardous to remain on the EU market. 

Let that sink in, no pun intended.

These proposals are a political choice to prioritise short-term profits for Big Polluters over children’s lives, people’s health, and the nature and ecosystems we need to survive.

Human health is at stake, and children are at particular risk – as they absorb substances more easily and are less able to excrete them. 

Pesticide exposure is linked to the development of childhood cancers, hormone disruption, neurodevelopmental impairments and birth defects. And prenatal and early childhood exposure can permanently alter development, with consequences that can be irreversible – and deadly.  

Under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, as well as the UN-declared human right to a healthy environment, all EU countries must commit to protecting children from environmental harm and ensure the highest attainable standard of health.

These principles must guide the work of EU institutions. 

Yet, instead of strengthening protections, the EU is moving backwards at a worrying speed. This is largely due to intense (and repeated) lobbying from multi-billion euro corporations, which includes the pesticides industry. Corporate chemical giants now spend €46m a year just to lobby the EU; that’s over 60 percent more than in 2020. 

Make it make sense

The incoherence of current EU policy is troubling. On the one hand, the EU Commission is celebrating its new Intergenerational Fairness Strategy – a framework that is meant to ensure today’s policies do not disadvantage future generations. On the other, the same institution is actively seeking to relax controls of harmful substances. 

Ripping up rules that protect people and the planet only benefits Big Polluters, industries that already make billions in profits at the expense of children’s health.

What’s more, an independent assessment found that the measures the EU institutions propose “will not accelerate innovations and authorisations”. In short, these proposals would actually make Europe less competitive.

Children’s rights and youth organisations have warned that deregulation exposes children to serious (and preventable) health risks. And the international scientific community recently stressed that robust environmental risk assessments cannot be optional.

Ultimately, Europe should widen and accelerate its access to pesticide-free alternatives. It must also support farmers in their efforts to transition away from pesticides, towards a more sustainable and resilient model.

So, what can be done? First, the EU must close the tap on pesticide use and production, and support farmers transitioning to safer alternatives. Second, it’s time for leaders to hold Big Polluters accountable for the damage they cause – not force the bill onto regular taxpayers and families harmed by these toxic substances.

Florence, Franck, and Isabelle’s children are among the hundreds of thousands already affected by pesticides. And they show that victims of pesticides are not just a statistic.

The ‘Food and Feed Safety Omnibus’ raises fundamental questions. Who exactly is the EU’s food policy supposed to protect? How many more children need to be harmed for politicians to act? And what kind of future do EU institutions want to build? 

Should pesticide protections be treated as obstacles to short-term profits, or should children be able to grow up safely? 

Politicians should reject this devastating Omnibus proposal and work instead to support the EU’s transition to safe, sustainable, and resilient farming.

]]> Inside Poland’s fake student scheme: cheap labour, bogus visas and Russian ties https://euobserver.com/239684/pro-russian-figures-linked-to-polish-universities-selling-paperwork-for-schengen-visas/ Thu, 01 Oct 2026 08:34:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=239684 In Poland, student status has become a sought-after commodity that employment agencies exploit for gains. Fake students cheaper for employers

Polish labour laws incentivise employment of students aged up to 26 under so-called agreements to perform a job. It means employers do not have to pay social security or health insurance contributions for them. The workers cost less than regular employees.

So, student status has become a sought-after commodity that employment agencies have exploited for gains.

A central figure in the case is Dariusz M., a school head in Sieradz detained by police in late May. When reporters from TVN24 posed as employers looking for a way to legalise the employment of foreign immigrants, M. offered to enrol them as students for 750 zloty (around €175) per person.

Prosecutors suspect him of participating in an organised group that allegedly issued around 2,500 false study certificates, costing the Polish state nearly six million zloty (more than €1.4m) in unpaid contributions.

Documents were often arranged by employment agencies with foreign workers unaware they had formally been enrolled at a school.

“In most cases, they do not even know they are involved in something illegal. They trust the employment agency,” said Rocio Flores, president of the Union of Latin American Workers in Poland.

When an inspection uncovers the fraud, the foreign workers face losing their jobs, residency problems and, in some cases, deportation. “We migrants suffer most as a result,” Flores said.

Inspections carried out by Poland’s social insurance authority confirmed there were many such cases.

In August, Dziennik Gazeta Prawna reported that Poland’s social insurance body (ZUS) stepped up inspections of companies employing foreigners with pupil or student status.

They reported that inspectors uncovered cases in which agencies pay schools for fake study certificates despite the worker having never attended classes, with Poland’s social welfare system losing out on millions of zloty.

Schools oblivious to study scam

Not all paperwork for fake students came from education institutions themselves. Some student cards and study certificates were forged in the name of real schools without their knowledge, as was the case of a Cosinus network branch in the town of Piaseczno.

Its head, Elżbieta Gotchold-Leśniewski, showed Onet reporters a file containing 62 forgeries found in various parts of Poland and had been issued to people from South America, Africa, Asia and Europe. “That is not my signature, and the school’s hologram is wrong too. ]]> AI chatbots turn users’ most intimate data into a potential goldmine for advertisers, researchers warn https://euobserver.com/239963/ai-chatbots-turn-users-most-intimate-data-into-a-potential-goldmine-for-advertisers-researchers-warn/ Thu, 01 Oct 2026 06:51:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=239963 Researchers found that even when users rejected non-essential cookies, Perplexity, DeepSeek, Gemini, Copilot, ChatGPT and Claude still connected to Google Ads.]]> Six out of nine of the most popular AI chatbots routinely exposed user input to third parties, new European research reveals.

Multiple chatbots disclosed sensitive user data to advertising companies through trackers – a piece of code used to identify and target users on the web with customised advertisements, which are widely used across the web.

And tech companies may have been able to link conversation summaries with personal identifiers, allowing users to be targeted based on their conversations with AI.

The researchers aimed to establish the connection between existing tracking technologies and AI advertising. “We basically connected the dots, and wanted to test whether and how AI bots integrate tracking and advertising services,” said Narseo Vallina-Rodriguez, who led the study.

Vallina-Rodriguez is part of a group of researchers who investigated the use of ad trackers in the most popular AI providers with colleagues at Imdea, a public research institute in Madrid.

Their findings warn of “tensions” between tech company practices and obligations to users under privacy laws.

Sensitive user-data shared 

“We already knew that tracking is pervasive, even without AI. But now you have the most super-invasive phenomena on the internet, which is AI,” said Itxaso Domínguez de Olazábal, a policy adviser at digital rights group Edri.

Users often share information about their health, psychological state, finances, and other intimate matters in AI prompts. The study shows how users who asked AI questions about such matters could have sensitive details summarised in a chat title shared with third parties. 

“Now, big tech has access to much more intimate information which users tell AI. It’s crazy, the details are so intimate. My friends ask AI bots about relationships, or they use ‘doctor AI’,” said Domínguez de Olazábal.

GDPR rules require companies to make clear how users’ data is harvested, but researchers question “ambiguous expressions” used to explain the role of trackers in T&Cs.

And the ePrivacy directive requires users to consent to cookies unless they are “strictly necessary”, but researchers found that even when users rejected non-essential cookies, AI bots Perplexity, DeepSeek, Gemini, Copilot, ChatGPT and Claude still connected to Google Ads.

All of the top nine most popular chatbots were found to integrate at least one third-party advertising or tracking service.

Consent and transparency ‘shortcomings’

A preview of the study, released in May, prompted the Spanish privacy watchdog AEPD to request for the European Data Protection Committee (EPDC) to share preliminary findings with European counterparts “for knowledge and assessment”.

The final paper, titled ‘Prompt like a Butterfly, Sting like a Tracker’, has been accepted for publication at an academic forum in Delft next year.

Findings “highlight tensions between current practices and obligations under the GDPR and ePrivacy Directive, exposing broader shortcomings in consent, access control, and transparency mechanisms,” the paper reads.

It reveals that Grok, operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI, exposed public links to conversations by default, allowing trackers to routinely access whole conversations, with TikTok also processing screenshots of Grok conversations.

  • The Ukrainian army stays in control of front lines, but safety in cities deteriorates.

  • Kyiv was on fire again as Russian attacks on cities intensify.

    • The Ukrainian army stays in control of front lines, but safety in cities deteriorates. The war has reached a stage in which two separate conflicts appear to be taking place simultaneously.

    While Ukraine is currently losing the battle in the air and its cities are continually suffering missile and strikes by jet drones, the situation on battlefields is far better.

    Last week, Denník N spent time in Ukraine with former chief of the general staff Daniel Zmeko. During the trip, reporters met commanding officers from several brigades and battalions operating from the Izium area to Zaporizhzhia, and all of them said they had the situation under control.

    The officers spoke about the accuracy of Russian maps, which they said did not correspond to reality. In some places, Russian soldiers are as far as 20 km from the locations where, according to the Kremlin, they are supposed to be.

    Northern flank of the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk agglomeration: This is a specific section of the front where the Ukrainian army has been reporting its advances only very slowly, while Ukrainian analysts have remained silent so as not to disclose anything sensitive. Russian bloggers, by contrast, are depicting the situation more closely to reality.

    Yet official Russian maps persist with utterly nonsensical lines. We do not know to what extent this is an effort to deceive domestic and foreign audiences, and to what extent they genuinely believe it in Moscow. It is worth looking at how the regime wants the situation to appear, and what it is really like.

    The first map in the overview was produced by the Russian state news agency RIA Novosti and depicts the area around Lyman, on the northern flank of the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk direction, as of 29 September. Lyman is shown as occupied in the middle of the map. The map’s author also continues to insist that the Russian army had captured Sviatohirsk — at the tip of the red salient in the centre of the map — and that Russia controls the entire, now non-existent salient with the village of Novoselivka at its centre. Yet Russian outlets Rybar and Two Majors write that fighting is taking place on the Zherebets river around the villages of Terny — on the far right of the map — and Yampil.

    The following map is much closer to reality. According to it, the front line roughly follows the Zherebets river, which corresponds to Rybar’s claims.

    Rybar’s map looks like this:

    Kupiansk direction: The city of Kupiansk is a similar case to Sviatohirsk. Putin declared it captured in August last year. And once the commander-in-chief had declared this, his news agency continued to draw the map as though it were true. Kupiansk is shown as occupied in its centre, but there are further inaccuracies.

    For example, the Kremlin agency claims that the Ukrainian bridgehead on the eastern bank of the Oskil river south of the city no longer exists. Ukrainians do face major difficulties supplying it, and various analysts have repeatedly warned of an impending disaster, but the Russian map is nevertheless hopelessly inaccurate.

    Also note the small town of Borova at the bottom centre. RIA Novosti also shows it as occupied, although this is not the case.

    This time, we will compare the Russian agency’s data with a map by Ukrainian analysts at DeepStateUA, because they updated it on Tuesday to reflect a new advance by Ukrainian units north of Kupiansk — again in the centre of the map — near the village of Dvorichne. In recent weeks, they have succeeded in reducing the Russian bridgehead on the western bank of the Oskil; the change since the end of August is marked in blue. Borova is again at the bottom centre, while below Kupiansk is the Ukrainian bridgehead that Russia claims does not exist.

    Orikhiv: This is one of the places where Ukrainian officers said during reporters’ trip to Ukraine that Russian maps were particularly inaccurate.

    The Russian map is again from RIA Novosti and again ignores reality along the entire length of this section of the front. Its main target is the city of Zaporizhzhia, with a population of three quarters of a million, in the centre left, while the small town of Orikhiv, at the bottom centre, is a defensive hub.

    Putin’s news agency places soldiers roughly 12 km from the southern edge of Zaporizhzhia; in reality, they are around 24 km away. It shows Orikhiv as occupied and the Russian army advancing from the east towards the village of Novorozivka, north of Orikhiv.

    The OSINT project Playfra covers this area in the greatest detail. Its map appears to depict a different war altogether. Everywhere, Russian positions are significantly shifted compared with those shown by RIA Novosti.

    The differences have a simple explanation. On the western flank near Zaporizhzhia, the Kremlin agency simply ignores the successful counterattacks carried out by Ukrainians there this year. On the eastern flank, it uncritically accepts every claim by the Russian defence ministry and, with equal lack of scrutiny, considers captured every small village where a Russian soldier raised a flag during a suicidal mission, even several months ago. Although those soldiers have since been killed or captured, RIA Novosti acts as though they still control the village.

    Playfra also offers a more detailed view of the current fighting around Orikhiv, drawing on analyses by Ukrainian analyst Kostyantyn Mashovets.

    Of course, Russians too occasionally notice that they are living in a parallel reality. Most recently, the influential Aleksandr Kharchenko wrote about it:

    “Comparing our maps with Ukrainian ones can be shocking. The zones of control differ by dozens of kilometres,” he acknowledged, adding that both sides lie, although he focused specifically on false Russian reports.

    He described Russian soldiers who are the first to break into a village as heroes. But, according to him, wars are not won through heroism, but through a functioning system.

    “Errors in our maps and information arise because they rely on heroes. Everywhere a Russian soldier is sitting is considered our territory,” Kharchenko argued that this had to change because “our territory is only where a Russian soldier is sitting with food, water and ammunition. This is territory from which we can fight the enemy”.

    Kyiv was on fire again as relentless Russian attacks on cities intensify. In the capital, Russians particularly targeted energy infrastructure. “Not a single day has passed since the summer without the enemy attacking energy infrastructure. But this is the first such massive and complex attack since the end of the previous heating season,” Ukrainian PM Serhiy Koretskyi told NV.

    In addition to causing serious damage, the attacks on Kyiv and other cities killed at least five residents and injured another 14.

    President Volodymyr Zelensky also said that, thanks to the delivery of new surface-to-air missiles, five Russian ballistic missiles had been shot down.

    Rubikon published stats on destroyed Ukrainian drones, decoys being the second most prominent. Ukraine’s response is continuing in parallel with the Russian offensive against cities. But the stats currently weigh against Ukraine.

    While the effectiveness of Ukrainian air defence has fallen dramatically since the arrival of Russian jet drones, Russia has successfully shot down Ukrainian ones. For example, the recent large-scale drone raid on Moscow involved several hundred drones — and, according to some sources, more than 1,000 — but only 10 penetrated the airspace above the Russian capital.

    In this context, the Russian Rubikon unit published interesting statistics. Although it operates at and near the front, its data for September show that, of 827 Ukrainian drones hit, as many as 247 were Maya-type drones — unmanned decoys intended to deceive Russian air defences. They look very similar to FP-1 attack drones but, unlike them, carry no warhead.

    Russia’s defence ministry will not let go of the Armata: it wants to turn it into an air-defence system, drawing ridicule. Zvezda News is a media outlet directly controlled by the Russian defence ministry. On Monday evening, it published technical news on the long-forgotten T-14 Armata tank, which Russian propaganda had claimed would revolutionise tank warfare.

    Today, it is beyond any doubt that the project is dead and new information confirms this, but its authors presumably intended to convey precisely the opposite.

    “Rostec has upgraded the Russian T-14 Armata tank into a short-range air-defence system,” the report stated, citing military expert Oleg Shaladin.

    Further changes have already been made to the project, but even the brief list above makes it clear that the Armata is no longer intended to be a tank, but rather some kind of hybrid capable of fighting everything and nothing at the same time.

    Among others, the Russian Telegram channel Military Informant commented on the report, openly mocking it. It said Rostec had mixed together “all the old tales from 10 years ago” in its list of changes, but that in practice “the tank never got beyond parades and training grounds, because it was created for an entirely different war, which ultimately never happened. It became conceptually obsolete from the outset, without even having had the chance to fight”.

    Videos of the day

    Russia has lost another Tu-95MS strategic bomber. This is the 12th confirmed loss of this type — the Oryx website has not yet updated its figures, so it records only 11. According to available information, the aircraft crashed shortly after taking off from a base in Amur region. Six crew members were reportedly killed, while one survived with injuries. Armed with cruise missiles, the aircraft was probably heading for Olenya air base, from which Russia attacks Ukraine.

    Denník N wrote on Tuesday about the attack on the headquarters of the Ukrainian Academy of Sciences. A video has since emerged from the helmet camera of one of the firefighters involved in the rescue operation.

    What are the losses

    No update on Wednesday.

    • By Tuesday (22 September), Russia had verifiably lost 24,138 pieces of heavy equipment, compared with 24,098 on Monday (14 September). Of these, 19,105 (19,065) were destroyed by Ukrainians, 1,000 (1,000) were damaged, 1,194 (1,194) were abandoned by their crews and 2,839 (2,839) were captured by the Ukrainian army. This includes 4,448 (4,447) tanks, of which 3,353 (3,352) were destroyed in combat.

    • Ukraine lost 12,175 (12,143) pieces of equipment, including 9,579 (9,551) destroyed, 702 (698) damaged, 695 (695) abandoned and 1,199 (1,199) captured. This includes 1,464 (1,462) tanks, of which 1,125 (1,120) were destroyed in combat.

    Note: Neither side regularly reports its own deaths or equipment losses. Ukraine publishes daily figures for Russian casualties and destroyed equipment, which cannot be independently verified. In this overview, we use data from the Oryx project, which has compiled a list based exclusively on photographically documented equipment losses since the start of the war.

    ]]>         Let’s not allow AI firms to use fears of future dystopias to distract Europeans from existing problems https://euobserver.com/240465/while-ai-companies-keep-us-talking-about-the-future-were-ignoring-the-damage-theyre-doing-now/ Wed, 30 Sep 2026 14:17:26 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240465 As Big Tech companies dramatise rogue AI and China fears, the real fight is over who pays the price for today’s fraud, failures and job threats — and who pockets the productivity gains.]]> “Imagine a zombie that does not hunt you, but rings your doorbell and speaks so persistently and fluently that it finally arrives at a convincing argument for feeding it your brain.”

    Norway’s proposed legislation is seemingly comprehensive, covering property purchases and services connected to construction and property transactions.

    The UK has also announced a ban on advertising property in illegal Israeli settlements, after such property had been advertised at a London real-estate event.

    The problem is treating a spatial category as though the economic relationships producing it share the same boundary. We all know the world does not work like that.

    Kinnula, a municipality in central Finland, is now facing this reality: when money from the illegal settlement economy moves into public land in Europe. It is a small case, but it makes the problem unusually visible.
