A Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) case recently brought the issue to the fore, after a Tesco employee was fired for taking bakery items 40 minutes before they became free to staff.

The employee argued his dismissal was disproportionate but Tesco had demonstrated a consistent policy of dismissing staff for dishonest conduct regardless of the value involved.

The WRC found Tesco had complied with fair procedures under the Unfair Dismissals Act.

How common is employee theft?

It’s more common than you might think, according to Moira Grassick, chief operating officer at employment law and HR firm Peninsula Ireland.

“Theft is one of the most common conduct issues we see on our HR advice lines, so clearly it’s something that employers are navigating on a regular basis,” she says.

Michelle Halloran, independent HR consultant and workplace investigator, of Halloran HR Resolutions, says that employees have been dismissed in the past for taking a banana home without paying.

A banana? Is it really that big of a deal?

Such consequences might seem “very draconian” and “petty”, Halloran says, but big retailers can have thousands of employees.

“If you’ve got 10,000 employees and they’re all taking a banana home every day, you can see how that become a problem very quickly,” she says.

Most retailers often factor in such losses into their operating costs, Halloran says, though they aim primarily for a “zero-tolerance approach”.

Tesco worker sacked for taking bakery items before they became ‘free to staff’ loses unfair dismissal claim

What is a zero-tolerance approach?

A zero-tolerance approach against employee theft is a policy commonly adopted by retailers which outlines in writing what will not be tolerated, such as theft.

It is often preferred because it ensures rules are applied “fairly and consistently”, Grassick says.

“Once you start treating incidents on a case-by-case basis, the lines can quickly become blurred; how do you differentiate between a serious theft versus a minor case?

“Is there a specific item value that warrants dismissal over a disciplinary warning? And if each incident is judged separately, how do you prevent favouritism or bias from impacting the outcome?” she says.

Grassick says it is “vital” that employers have a clear policy in place that outlines exactly what will not be tolerated in the workplace, as well as clarifying the disciplinary consequences of that behaviour.

Some employers also include in these policies the right to search employee belongings on leaving work, Halloran says.

What are the consequences of an employee not adhering to a zero-tolerance policy?

It is often dismissal, Halloran says, adding that employers take any breach “very seriously” and often enforce the policy and disciplinary measures as a matter of principle.

If employees do not follow rules precisely, such as the Tesco employee who took bakery items 40 minutes before they became free to staff, they could lose their job.

For example, some employers allow workers to take a number of products each day for lunch, but might stipulate that they must be consumed on the premises.

“If they take them off the premises, that’s theft,” she says.

What about non-retail employers?

Very few companies outside of the retail sector have written policies on employee theft, Halloran says, which means they could have difficulty disciplining employees found taking toilet roll or office supplies.

Without such a policy, custom and practice or even an “unspoken perk of the job” can create problems, she says.

Anti-theft policies should set out clearly what the employer constitutes as theft, Halloran says, noting that people generally have “subjective attitudes when it comes to low-value items”.

If you’re still paying current account fees in an era of free banking, it might be time to have the talk.

Once upon a time, a relationship with a bank was exclusive. Maybe you got together when you were younger, you trusted them with your salary and your savings, maybe you even took out a mortgage together. Your current account did the basics, such as paying the bills, receiving and dispensing cash, and offering access to a bit of foreign currency for your holidays.

Fees

A number of new digital banks are now offering Irish customers current accounts with no monthly fees. Monzo, Revolut, Bunq and N26 do not charge a fixed maintenance charge for their basic accounts.

These are financial technology or “fintech” companies so there are no branches; you bank exclusively through an app.

From Revolut to Money Jar: What are your options among new digital banking players?

The digital banks might offer free current account banking but there can be some limitations, depending on how you bank.

If you need physical cash regularly, the ease and cost of getting it is something to consider before ditching your old bank. The no branch/cash thing is one of the main reasons people who sign up to a neobank still keep some connection with a pillar bank on the side.

With the neobanks, you can use your physical or virtual debit card to pay at the till but, unlike AIB, Bank of Ireland, PTSB, EBS and a credit union current account, you can’t generally get cash back.

If you need a regular stream of fivers for birthday cards, bake sales and the tuck shop, that can be a pain.

You can take your neobank card to an ATM but withdrawals may come at a cost.

With a Revolut standard free account, you can withdraw up to €200 per rolling month, or five withdrawals, whichever comes first. Thereafter, you will be charged a fee of 2 per cent of anything withdrawn over those limits.

Monzo allows you withdraw up to €300 fee-free per rolling 30 days, with a 2.5 per cent charge on amounts withdrawn after that.

Monzo offers instant transfers too, though the usefulness of this feature will be limited by how many Monzo customers there are in your network.

Why now is the time to review your mortgage

There’s now Zippay too. That’s the instant payments system launched recently by the pillar banks – AIB, Bank of Ireland and PTSB.

The one big advantage for Zippay is that it’s in the app of these three banks, so it has potential to reach more than five million customers. And using it will spare them having to keep toggling to Revolut. Monzo will struggle to compete with Revolut and Zippay on instant payments.

Joint accounts

Being in a couple is where all these new current account options can get a bit messy.

If you have an account with a pillar bank and a neobank, and your partner has an account with a pillar bank and neobank, that’s four different current accounts.

If you are both maintaining a current account with a traditional bank, you could be paying up to €96 each a year each in account maintenance fees, or €192 between you. That’s a Netflix subscription right there.

Biggest difference to your pension pot is not how much money you put in

If you feel you need to hang on to a traditional bank current account for the sake of the odd cash withdrawal or lodgement, you’ll save some money by opting for a joint account here.

Like the main banks, all the neobanks offer free joint current accounts too.

If you do decide to change current account providers, there’s the matter of switching all your direct debits from one current account to another. Ask your new bank if they provide a switching service.

]]>DragonImages<![CDATA[Eir seen increasing dividends as need for fibre investment eases]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/09/30/eir-seen-increasing-dividends-as-need-for-fibre-investment-eases/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/09/30/eir-seen-increasing-dividends-as-need-for-fibre-investment-eases/Wed, 30 Sep 2026 05:00:00 +0000Eir may increase dividends to its controlling shareholder, French telecoms billionaire Xavier Niel, and its joint venture fibre network partner to as much as €225 million per year, as it largely completes investment in high-speed broadband roll-out, according to Fitch.

The group paid an average of €181 million of dividends to shareholders and its fibre network partner, Paris-based private-equity firm InfraVia Capital, over the past two years.

Eir’s wholesale broadband business is facing mounting competitive pressure resulting from “overbuild” of fibre by industry players in recent times, including Siro, a joint venture between ESB and Vodafone, and Virgin Media, Fitch said as it withdrew its coverage of the company.

A spokeswoman for Eir confirmed that the company has moved from being covered by three ratings agencies to two from now on, Moody’s and S&P Global.

The group saw its wholesale broadband base fall by 34,000 subscriptions to 429,000 in the 12 months to the end of June. However, its retail broadband and mobile customers grew.

While Eir reported that its €2.89 billion net debt at the end of June equated to 4.7 times its earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (ebitda), Fitch’s methodology put the leverage ratio at 5.2. This gives Eir limited headroom compared with the 5.5 level where Fitch would ordinarily consider downgrading the group’s creditworthiness.

“Leverage headroom has been constrained by peak network investment and competitive pressure in the wholesale segment. Eir, the former State monopoly which has been through seven changes in control in the past 27 years, has distributed about €2.29 billion in dividends to its owners since Niel led the takeover in April 2018.

A Niel investment vehicle now owns more than 70 per cent of the business, following the exit of hedge fund Davidson Kempner as a shareholder in 2024 and fellow US minority investor Anchorage selling back some of its stock months later.

However, Niel, whose family is invested telecoms businesses in 20 countries across Europe and Latin America that are currently generating about €24 billion of annual revenue, told The Irish Times in an interview two years ago that he and co-investors “always invest as much as we [take] in dividends”.

“We share what we do between three. First, the company and the people working in the company. Second, the customers. And third, the shareholder. It’s always what we do in all our countries and it’s one of our big secrets,” he said.

The French billionaire who will hold on to Eir ‘until the day I die’

Shareholder payouts have decreased in recent years, after several large dividend payments under Niel’s control, including €800 million in dividends in 2022.

The large payout was underpinned as Eir sold off a 49.9 per cent stake in its wholesale broadband subsidiary, Fibre Networks Ireland (FNI), to InfraVia. Net proceeds from the stake sale and FNI subsequently raising debt, totalled €1.2 billion.

Eir-controlled FNI began paying dividends to InfraVia relating to its minority stake in the joint venture in 2023.

“We expect FNI to pay dividends to minority shareholders of €35 million-€45 million annually in 2026-2029,” said Fitch, adding that it sees normal Eir shareholder dividends amount to €150 million to €180 million annually over the same period.

The Eir spokeswoman said the group has no current plans in relation to debt or refinancing, but keeps its position under ongoing review “as part of its normal financial management”.

]]><![CDATA[Site next to Square in Tallaght with planning permission for 199 apartments seeks €5.9m]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/property/commercial-property/2026/09/30/site-next-to-square-in-tallaght-with-planning-permission-for-199-apartments-seeks-59m/https://www.irishtimes.com/property/commercial-property/2026/09/30/site-next-to-square-in-tallaght-with-planning-permission-for-199-apartments-seeks-59m/Wed, 30 Sep 2026 04:35:00 +0000A range of parties including developers, institutional investors and the Land Development Agency may be interested in the opportunity presented by the sale of a 1.19-hectare (2.94-acre) site at Tallaght Town Centre in Tallaght, Dublin 24.

Located immediately adjacent to The Square shopping centre and within a short walk of both Tallaght University Hospital and TUD’s Tallaght campus, the former Woodies site has full planning permission for a residential-led mixed-use scheme and is being offered to the market by agent Hooke & MacDonald at a guide price of €5.9 million.

The disposal of the property is being conducted on the instructions of John Healy and Myles Kirby of Kroll joint receivers over certain assets of Ravensbrook Ltd, a company headed by Siobhán Quinlan, a property investor and the wife of financier Derek Quinlan, John Gordon, with an address in Monaco, and Michael Quinlan, with an address in Castleknock.

While Ravensbrook’s directors had been seeking originally to develop as many as 326 apartments on the site, that plan never came to fruition. The receivers commissioned a planning application earlier this year, and in May secured permission on appeal from An Coimisiún Pleanála for the development of 199 apartments along with 17 commercial units and a 58-space basement car park.

The residential accommodation is to be distributed across two blocks of up to seven storeys in height. Block A includes 49 senior-living apartments and communal amenity facilities, while Block B comprises 150 apartments. The approved units comprise a mix of studio, one-bedroom, two-bedroom and three-bedroom apartments.

The approved commercial accommodation consists of 17 units with a combined area of 2,123sq m (22,851sq ft) which would be suitable for healthcare, retail, cafe, pharmacy, childcare and neighbourhood service uses.

The site’s €5.9 million guide price represents just a fraction of the €20 million that developer Bernard McNamara paid for it at the height of the Celtic Tiger era. McNamara’s company, Laytar, acquired the property from a group of investors assembled at the time by Derek Quinlan. A plan to develop 350 apartments on the site never materialised and the property was put back on the market in 2016 for €4.5 million.

Commenting on the site’s arrival to the market now, Donald McDonald of Hooke & MacDonald said: “Belgard Square East represents a rare opportunity to acquire a fully permitted mixed-use development site of scale in one of Dublin’s most important town centre locations.

“With planning permission in place for 199 apartments, commercial accommodation and a highly accessible location beside The Square shopping centre and the Luas, we expect strong interest from developers, investors and housing providers.”

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3443799/">
   <title>Russischer Angriff auf Brücke in Kiew</title>
   <description>Nach Angaben von Bürgermeister Witali Klitschko haben am Donnerstag zwei russische Drohnen eine wichtige Brücke in der ukrainischen Hauptstadt Kiew getroffen. Der öffentliche Verkehr über die Brücke wurde eingeschränkt, so Klitschko. Der Zustand der Brücke werde untersucht. Zudem gab es laut Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj einen Angriff auf eine Schule, verletzt worden sei dabei niemand. Bereits am Mittwoch soll laut ukrainischen Angaben das Gelände einer Atomforschungsanlage in Kiew getroffen und ein Brand ausgelöst worden sein.</description>

A group of prominent Polish businesspeople have announced that they are investing in a project to develop small modular nuclear reactors being led by the country’s richest man, Michał Sołowow.

Among them are Rafał Brzoska, founder of delivery giant InPost, and Mati Staniszewski, CEO of ElevenLabs, a leading artificial intelligence firm.

The group is investing 500 million zloty (€114 million) in Sołowow’s Synthos Green Energy (SGE), which, together with 1.35 billion zloty from foreign investors, will secure the company’s financing for the next two years as it seeks to roll out BWRX-300 reactors in Poland, Central and Eastern Europe and the UK.

As a European SMR development platform headquartered in Warsaw, Poland’s energy security is of special importance to us.

We are proud to announce that today our founder, Michał Sołowow, unveiled a PLN 500 million investment by a group of leading Polish entrepreneurs in SGE’s… pic.twitter.com/J2SerVjIlG

— SGE (@SGE_Nuclear) September 30, 2026

The investment, which was formally announced at a business conference in Warsaw on Wednesday, comes as Sołowow seeks to expand his nuclear project beyond SGE’s troubled partnership with Polish state energy giant Orlen, where disagreements have delayed plans to build SMRs in Poland.

Alongside Brzoska and Staniszewski, the other new investors are Dariusz Gałęzewski, co-founder of drinks maker Oshee; Krzysztof Pawiński, CEO of food company Maspex; Michał Brański of media group Wirtualna Polska; and Michał Wypychewicz of ZPUE, the largest manufacturer of transformer stations in Europe.

“They invested their own private funds because they understood the problem and then believed in the concept and the solution,” Sołowow told Business Insider Polska.

 

SMRs, which are prefabricated in factories before being installed on site, are seen by their proponents as a fast and cost-effective way of installing nuclear capacity.

In July, SGE announced plans to build 14 BWRX-300 reactors with a combined capacity of 4.2 gigawatts (GW) across three sites in the UK, which it said would generate enough electricity to meet 11% of the country’s demand. The company also hopes to deploy up to 26 reactors across six locations in Poland.

The BWRX-300 is a 300-megawatt water-cooled small modular reactor. Construction of the first ever unit began in Canada in 2025, with completion planned for 2029 and commercial operation expected in 2030.

Synthos Green Energy, a firm owned by Polish billionaire Michał Sołowow, has announced plans to build 14 small modular nuclear reactors in the UK.

It says that the £35 billion project could deliver enough power to meet 11% of the UK’s demand https://t.co/YTMIzYERuJ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2026

Brzoska said that developing SMR technology “is an investment in Poland’s future”, because without “reliable, predictable and competitively priced energy…it is difficult to talk seriously about further growth in industry, data centres, artificial intelligence, automation or modern logistics”.

Staniszewski, whose company recently received an $11 million investment from Poland’s state-owned National Development Bank (BGK) to establish an AI development centre in Poland, said lower electricity prices were important for the sector.

SGE notes that demand for electricity is set to rise 40% in Poland over the next 14 years, according to grid operator PSE. Electricity prices have risen rapidly in recent years and are now the second most expensive in the European Union in relation to the cost of living.

Poland has recorded the EU's third-fastest rise in household electricity prices this year.

The country now also has the bloc’s second-most-expensive electricity, when taking cost of living into account https://t.co/WNLdCfOP16

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2025

Poland remains the EU’s most coal-dependent country, with more than half of its electricity generated from coal. Over the past decade, however, the country has diversified its energy mix, with the share of renewable energy sources tripling to nearly 30% in 2025.

Poland plans to reduce its reliance on coal further, including through the construction of its first nuclear power plant (of the traditional type, not an SMR). The 3.75-gigawatt project is scheduled to be commissioned in 2036.

Sołowow has also been pursuing the deployment of SMRs in Poland through Orlen Synthos Green Energy (OSGE), a joint venture between SGE and state energy giant Orlen, Poland’s largest company, to develop BWRX-300 reactors in Poland.

OSGE is seeking a so-called contract for difference (CfD) framework, an agreement with a state that guarantees a fixed price for electricity and helps shield developers from market swings, covering 14 reactors at three sites.

Polish state energy firm Orlen has announced an agreement to build the country’s first small modular nuclear reactor (SMR).

It says Poland will be the first country in Europe to deploy an SMR developed by US-based firm GE Hitachi Nuclear Energy https://t.co/MPWXS3qZ1d

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 28, 2025

The project, however, has been delayed by disagreements between the two shareholders. Sołowow told Business Insider Polska that they reached an agreement last month that would allow construction of two reactors to move forward, but said he regretted entering into the partnership with Orlen.

“I find it deeply regrettable, because it is precisely due to Orlen’s unnecessary involvement that we are discussing this project in political terms, even though it is not a political project,” he said.

Sołowow has argued that a private-sector model can shorten construction times and improve cost control compared with traditional state-led nuclear projects.

At the same time, he has highlighted the importance of the state’s role in implementing the project, saying its success depends on coordination between private investors and state policy. This includes contracts for difference, administrative procedures and the preparedness of the nuclear regulator.

Activists in Poland have launched what they say is the world’s first delivery locker that provides women with abortion pills, access to which is normally tightly restricted.

They have placed the device opposite parliament in Warsaw, a location intended to send a message to the politicians who have made Poland’s abortion laws among the strictest in the world.

The locker (called an “abortomat” in Polish, combining the words aborcja, meaning abortion, and automat, meaning an automatic machine) has been launched by Women Help Women (WHW), a global organisation that provides “self-managed abortion”, and Abortion Dream Team (ADT), a Polish activist group.

They emphasise that the installation “is completely real [and] not an artistic performance”. It consists of 22 numbered lockers and a numeric keypad. Women who have contacted WHM seeking an abortion are given a six-digit PIN code that opens one of the doors, inside which is a package containing the pills.

Recipients can either take the pills at home or do so in a specially prepared space opened last year by ADT and where the locker is located.

 

The activists emphasise that such delivery mechanisms for abortion pills are particularly important in Poland because of the country’s highly restrictive laws.

Abortions are only allowed in two circumstances: if pregnancy is the result of a crime (such as rape or incest) or if it threatens the mother’s life or health. As a result, only 851 legal terminations took place in Poland last year.

However, activist groups such as WHW, ADT and Women on Web (WOW) say that they help tens of thousands of women in Poland obtain abortions each year through other means, in particular by providing pills.

But they face legal risks for doing so: assisting someone in obtaining an unlawful abortion is a crime punishable by up to three years in prison. In 2023, ABW activist Justyna Wydrzyńska was convicted of that offence. Two years later, the sentence was annulled on a technicality and a new trial was ordered.

Polish activist Justyna Wydrzyńska, who was convicted for providing abortion pills to a pregnant woman, has succeeded in having the conviction overturned on appeal.

However, the case will now return to the lower court, where it will be heard again https://t.co/U3J5FmXdMw

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 14, 2025

“The abortomat transforms a closely guarded, criminalised procedure into something as simple as picking up a package,” wrote ADT. “A door that opens when all others have slammed shut.”

They say that the machine is intended for women who have an urgent medical need that means they cannot wait for the several days it takes to deliver pills by post, or who are in abusive, controlling relationships that make postal delivery unsafe.

Wydrzyńska’s conviction came after the husband of a woman she helped obtain abortion pills found them and reported the case to the police. However, although assisting a woman in obtaining an unlawful abortion is an offence, the woman who had the abortion is not criminally liable.

“The abortomat is not a human being, and the person collecting the pills, in accordance with the regulations, is not breaking the law,” said Wydrzyńska, quoted by news website Wirtualna Polska. WHW and ADT do not collect any personal information from women using the service.

Under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which ruled from 2015 to 2023, the abortion law was tightened and was strictly enforced.

In December 2023, a new, more liberal coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk came to power, promising to liberalise the abortion law. However, it has so far failed to pass any such legislation.

In 2024, a move to decriminalise abortion assistance up to the 12th week of pregnancy was rejected by parliament, after the most conservative element of Tusk’s coalition joined the right-wing opposition in voting against it.

Tusk subsequently admitted that it would be impossible during the current parliament to soften abortion laws. Instead, his government issued guidelines on when and how abortions can be carried out, with the aim of ensuring that doctors and prosecutors “take the women’s side” when making decisions on the issue.

Poland’s inflation accelerated to an annual rate of 4.0% in September, up from 3.4% a month earlier, driven primarily by higher fuel prices amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East and the end of Polish government subsidies that kept down prices at the pump.

The development means that inflation has now risen above the upper bound of 3.5% set by the National Bank of Poland (NBP), which aims to keep the figure at 2.5%, plus or minus one percentage point. Analysts say that an interest rate hike by the NBP is now more likely.

The new preliminary inflation figures from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, show that prices in September were 4% higher than a year earlier, the fastest rise since June 2025. On a monthly basis, prices in September were up 0.7% from August.

The rise was caused in particular by the price of fuel for private transport, which was up 36.1% on a year earlier and 9.2% from the previous month. Energy prices also rose, with electricity, gas and other fuels up 4.9% year-on-year and 0.9% month-on-month.

To shield consumers from the energy crisis triggered by US and Israeli attacks on Iran, Poland has twice introduced temporary measures to curb petrol station prices, including daily price caps and cuts in VAT and excise duty. The system was in place from March to June and again during the the last two weeks of August.

The government has been under pressure from the opposition and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki to reintroduce the subsidies. However, it argues that Nawrocki’s decision to block a proposed windfall tax on fuel companies makes the measures harder to fund

 

Food and non-alcoholic beverage prices provided some offset, falling 0.5% from a year earlier, although they edged up 0.1% from August. Analysts, however, expect food prices to rise later in the year to reflect lower agricultural yields.

According to GUS’s own estimates, also published on Wednesday, the grain harvest came in 5% lower compared to the last season. This will, in turn, “push the CPI index higher in the coming months”, wrote Erste Bank.

The breach of the upper end of the central bank’s inflation target and the 4% threshold could influence the stance of the NBP’s Monetary Policy Council (RPP), prompting it to hike rates, added Erste Bank analysts.

A Polish painting looted by Nazi Germany during World War Two, and which once hung in an SS officers’ club, has been returned by its owner, who donated it to the National Museum in Warsaw.

“History is coming home,” said culture minister Marta Cienkowska, celebrating the return of Alfred Wierusz-Kowalski’s Winter – Napoleon’s Retreat from Moscow, which she described as “one of the most significant wartime losses in Polish painting”.

Her ministry is responsible for seeking the return of tens of thousands of artworks and other cultural items that were looted during the war and remain missing.

Kolejny sukces restytucyjny! Odzyskaliśmy jedną z cenniejszych i najbardziej znanych strat wojennych malarstwa polskiego. Obraz „Zima – Odwrót Napoleona spod Moskwy” Alfreda Wierusza-Kowalskiego trafił dziś do zbiorów Muzeum Narodowego w Warszawie.

To efekt naszej współpracy z… pic.twitter.com/Y0wDIBgIGG

— Ministerstwo Kultury i Dziedzictwa Narodowego (@kultura_gov_pl) September 28, 2026

Wierusz-Kowalski, who was active in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, was a renowned realist painter whose work often featured animals alongside people. His Winter – Napoleon’s Retreat from Moscow had, by the 1930s, become part of the collection of Andrzej Rotwand, a wealthy banker and industrialist.

In June 1939, it was featured in an exhibition organised by the Society for the Encouragement of Fine Arts in Warsaw, which occupied the building that is now the famous Zachęta National Gallery of Art.

However, the exhibition was brought to an abrupt end when Nazi Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. The works on display, along with other items from the gallery, were seized by the occupiers, with many used to decorate the offices and apartments of German officials.

Winter – Napoleon’s Retreat from Moscow was displayed in a club for high-ranking SS and police officers located in Warsaw’s Blanka Palace. The same building also housed Warsaw’s German-installed commissioner, Helmut Otto, and mayor, Ludwig Leist.

 

No information has been released as to the fate of the painting in the immediate aftermath of the war. However, it eventually came into the possession of Ewa Tsonis, who has now handed it back.

Speaking at a ceremony in the National Museum in Warsaw, Tsonis said that her late father, Michał Stefan Koryzna, had purchased the painting in the 1960s from Desa, a major gallery and auction house, in the city of Kraków.

“I grew up with this painting. It was greatly appreciated and loved in our family,” she said. However, after recently conducting research into the painting’s history, she became aware of its provenance and notified the culture ministry.

Ewa Tsonis (right) alongside the painting with culture minister Marta Cienkowska (centre) and the director of the national museum in Warsaw, Agnieszka Lajus

Experts from the National Museum in Warsaw confirmed the identity of the painting, which remains in good condition and in its original frame. Tsonis then donated the work to the museum.

“Restitution is not possible without the cooperation of many people and institutions – both on the side of the state and on the part of the owners of the works,” said Cienkowska, who thanked Tsonis for her “incredibly responsible and civic-minded attitude”.

“Such attitudes are still rare but, because we constantly talk about restitution – we search for lost works and strive to recover them – we are increasingly approached by people who own lost objects and feel a sense of responsibility for cultural heritage.”

Cienkowska noted that the culture ministry has so far secured the return of over 920 works, with around 200 more restitution cases currently underway in 18 countries.

Germany has agreed to return to Poland a collection of 73 medieval documents that were looted during WWII.

The culture minister has hailed it as "the most important and valuable return of stolen cultural heritage in modern Polish history" https://t.co/GxHQ8A0jyr

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 1, 2025

However, that is still just a small fraction of the over 60,000 missing items listed in the ministry’s database of missing works, which includes seven further paintings by Wierusz-Kowalski.

Two other works from Rotwand’s collection – Italian Woman by Anna Bilińska and Mother with Children by Kazimierz Alchimowicz – were also hung in the SS officers’ club during the war and today remain missing.

Poland has in recent years stepped up efforts to secure the return of historical and cultural items looted during the German and Soviet occupations.

In 2022, it appealed to UNESCO for help in securing the return of cultural items that remain missing after being looted by Nazi Germany. It also launched a campaign seeking the return of thousands of items that ended up in Russia after the war.

Poland is changing the procedures under which its military can fire upon foreign aircraft, citing the “growing threat from Russia”. Visual identification of targets will no longer be required, with other forms of data to be used instead.

The move follows a series of violations of Polish airspace over the last year by Russian drones, a missile and a helicopter, as well as Russia’s increasing use of jet-powered drones to attack targets in Ukraine close to the Polish border.

To także odpowiedź na rosnące zagrożenie ze strony Rosji, doświadczenia wojny w Ukrainie…

“In the coming days, the defence minister will change the procedures for firing by Polish planes and helicopters at objects flying to us from the direction of Russia,” announced deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk on Monday, quoted by news service Defence24.

The change, as Tomczyk explained in a statement later issued on social media, will shift requirements away from requiring visual identification of foreign aerial objects and towards so-called “positive identification”.

The latter involves identifying an object based on a combination of several other, non-visual sources of information, such as using radar and other sensors to determine its speed, altitude, trajectory and flight parameters, as well as a lack of IFF (identification friend or foe) from an object.

 

Tomczyk said that the change was being made based on the “conclusions from recent weeks” made by the operational commander of Poland’s armed forces, General Ireneusz Nowak.

It is a “response to the growing threat from Russia, experiences from the war in Ukraine, and the emergence of new air attack means – primarily fast jet drones and cruise missiles in the case of which the time for reaction is very brief”, added Tomczyk.

The minister said that positive identification would only be issued when there is a “sufficiently high degree of certainty in determining what we are dealing with”. He noted that accurate target identification is particularly crucial in peacetime, when there are civilian aircraft in Polish airspace.

The change will mean “not less identification, but a different way of conducting it: faster and based on data from multiple sources”.

“Until now, we have not utilised these [non-visual identification] capabilities because they are typically reserved for a state of war or martial law,” said Tomczyk.

Several early medieval Arabic silver coins have been found in a forest near Elbląg in northern Poland. Experts believe they may have belonged to merchants travelling to or from the Viking Age port of Truso, which was situated nearby.

The silver dirhams date back around 1,200 years, to the first half of the ninth century, before the founding of the Polish state. They may have remained in circulation until the turn of the 10th/11th century, the time of the settlement’s collapse.

The discovery of the “new treasure” was announced last week by the Archaeological and Historical Museum in Elbląg. It did not reveal who had unearthed them, but said that the find had taken place during a legal search in a forest near the town of Młynary, just east of Elbląg.

After conservation and processing work, the coins will be included in the collection of the museum, whose archaeologists will also visit the site hoping for further finds.

The museum’s Jakub Jagodziński told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that the find consists of “six early medieval Arabic dirhams and two fragments of these silver coins”. He said that they are provisionally dated to the first half of the 9th century, but a more precise estimate will be possible after they are processed.

 

The coins could have belonged to merchants travelling along the routes leading to or from Truso or to Prussian guards who later collected tolls on these routes, Jagodziński explained.

Truso was a Viking Age port of trade set up by the Scandinavians on the shores of lake Druzno near the Vistula river delta. Established by the late 7th century and active until the early 11th century, its location enabled trade extending towards Kyivan Rus, Byzantium and the Islamic world.

Historians knew of Truso’s existence because of the account of the Anglo-Saxon traveller Wulfstan of Hedeby. Centuries-long efforts to find the precise site proved fruitless until it was finally discovered in the early 1980s by the young archaeologist Marek Jagodziński, Jakub’s father.

Finds of Arab coins in Poland are not unprecedented. A silver deposit was discovered in 1986 on the site of Truso itself, consisting of 11 complete coins and five fragments. Coins found there were minted in places including Baghdad and Damascus, according to the Medievalists.net website.

More recently, in 2024, a fragment of an early medieval Arabic dirham was found during renovations of an old manor house on the Baltic coast in northwestern Poland.

In transactions involving dirhams, it was the value of the silver that mattered, so the coins were often broken into pieces, archaeologist Grzegorz Kurka told PAP.

“Therefore, when hoards of Arab coins are discovered in Poland, they are divided into several pieces. Whole coins are also found, but much less frequently,” he explained.

Poland has proposed that, if the United States grants Ukraine permission to produce its own missiles for Patriot air-defence systems, the factory could be located on Polish territory to ensure its security.

The news was revealed by deputy defence minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, who also confirmed that Poland would seek to establish a Patriot servicing and production facility even if it does not host Ukraine’s.

Poland wants to host Patriot production

Poland has proposed that the US and Ukraine launch joint production of Patriot missiles. Warsaw is citing security concerns and is proposing to host the facility in Poland instead of Ukraine:

“If such a factory is planned to be built in… pic.twitter.com/syCkNt0o0V

— Belsat in English (@Belsat_Eng) September 27, 2026

Patriot missile systems have been a key part of Ukraine’s defence against Russian aerial attacks. However, Kyiv has suffered from a shortage of missiles used in the system, prompting President Volodymyr Zelensky to appeal to allies to transfer their interceptors as well as to allow Ukraine to produce them itself.

US President Donald Trump initially told Zelensky at a meeting in July that “we are gonna give you a licence to make Patriots”. However, he then backtracked on that offer later the same month.

But, following weeks of uncertainty, on Friday last week Zelensky claimed that Trump had personally told him he had made a “final decision” to approve a licence for Ukraine to produce Patriot missiles. Washington has not confirmed that development.

 

Asked about the issue on Saturday, Sobkowiak-Czarnecka told broadcaster TVN, “let’s see if it happens”. However, she added that, “we proposed that, if such a factory is planned to be built in Ukraine, we propose building it in Poland, so that it would be in the so-called safe territory”.

Poland is already the primary hub for military equipment, goods and people being transported in and out of its eastern neighbour.

Sobkowiak-Czarnecka added that, regardless of where the plant serving Ukraine is located, Poland would also still seek to establish a facility for servicing and, eventually, production of Patriots.

“What my interlocutors in Washington confirmed is that, even if such a decision is made regarding Ukraine, it does not change our efforts and does not rule out consent for Poland,” she said. Sobkowiak-Czarnecka was in Washington last week for talks with US officials.

In May this year, another deputy defence minister, Cezary Tomczyk, told TVN that Poland had “received preliminary approval from the US State Department to produce missiles for Patriot systems”.

The Polish government has confirmed that it has transferred Patriot missiles to Ukraine following opposition criticism

It also released a list of all military donations to Ukraine since 2022, showing that the former PiS government gave much more equipment https://t.co/8BmDy5BjiB

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2026

In 2018, as part of its Wisła air defence programme, Poland signed a $4.75bn contract to purchase Patriot launchers and missiles from the US.

In October 2023, the first Patriot systems procured from the US were deployed at Warsaw Babice airport. In December 2025, Poland announced full operational readiness of its US-supplied Integrated Battle Command System (IBCS), an air-defence network that includes Patriot missile batteries.

Poland also has an agreement to domestically produce launchers for Patriot systems through cooperation between Polish state-owned defence contractor Huta Stalowa Wola SA and US defence giant Raytheon.

Poland has announced a $1.2bn deal that will see a Polish state-owned defence firm manufacture 48 launchers for Patriot missile systems domestically in cooperation with US defence giant Raytheon https://t.co/PQOjKvhqYM

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2024

The issue of Ukraine’s need for more Patriot missiles caused domestic political controversy in Poland earlier this year, when the right-wing opposition reacted angrily to reports that the government had handed over some interceptors to Ukraine.

In July, the government confirmed that it had done so. However, Prime Minister Donald Tusk later revealed that only five missiles had been transferred to Ukraine.

In late July, the Center for Strategic and International Studies reported that the Iran war had depleted America’s stockpile of Patriot missiles to 800 interceptors from roughly 2,300 before the war began.

Last week, Germany’s defence minister, Boris Pistorius, confirmed that his country has also proposed that it could manufacture interceptors and perhaps even entire Patriot systems.

Of course, darling: Richard E Grant simply must play David Bliss, the blinkered, posho patriarch at the centre of Noel Coward’s drawing room comedy, Hay Fever. This is how I imagine the casting conversations went, anyway. Shockingly, E Grant – everyone’s favourite aristo-portrayer – has until now never starred in a Coward play, so here is his moment. He is delicious as the delusional novelist in Emily Burns’ Hay Fever, the latest proof that Coward is still more than capable of summing up our 21st century idiosyncrasies fifty odd years after his death. 

You think these people are too flatly ridiculous to exist, and then you remember you know countless people like them. We’re in the Bliss household in the village of Cookham, Berkshire, where retired actress Judith Bliss is wafting around declaring that she is to make a return to the stage, although you suspect she says the same thing every day. On 25 September 1978, John Peel played Teenage Kicks, the debut single from The Undertones, on his Radio 1 evening show. Two minutes and 28 seconds later, in a brazen breach of BBC protocol, he played the same song for a second time, telling listeners “it doesn’t get much better than this”. 

I recently had an ‘instant replay’ moment of my own, driving on the Route Napoleon in the French Alps. This glorious road was used for the car chase in Goldeneye, with James Bond (Pierce Brosnan) manhandling an Aston Martin DB5, pursued by Xenia Onatopp in a Ferrari F355. The most spectacular section weaves through a series of steeply stacked hairpins, then clings to the cliff edge, cutting through natural arches in the jagged limestone rock.

It’s a stretch of tarmac so dramatic, challenging and exhilarating that, when I reached a roundabout, I couldn’t resist turning around and immediately doing it all again. Because it really doesn’t get much better than this, whether you’re driving a blue-blooded supercar or a battery-electric Kia. 

A new kind of electric performance 

If that sounds a bit hyperbolic, take note that the EV4 GT is not a common-or-garden Kia. Indeed, with dual motors, all-wheel drive, bigger brakes, adaptive dampers, electronic torque vectoring, Kia’s Virtual Gear Shift system and Pirelli P Zero tyres, it has aspirations to be a proper hot hatchback.

In recent years, ever-tighter legislation and emissions targets have made such cars into an endangered species. Many have been killed off with no successor in sight, among them the Ford Focus ST, Hyundai i30 N, Renault Megane RS and Honda Civic Type R. For somebody who got his teenage kicks driving hot hatches, this decline has been sad to see. 

Thankfully, a new breed of electric hot hatches has begun to emerge. If you want something supermini-sized, you can consider the Alpine A290 GTS, Vauxhall Corsa GSE or Peugeot 208 GTI. And at the top end of the market, there is the impressive Hyundai Ioniq 5 N, which resembles a hatchback but has the stature of an SUV.

Until now, though, no credible EV contender has targeted the hot hatch heartland inhabited by the Volkswagen Golf GTI. That’s where the Kia comes in. 

Kia EV GT prices and spec

At £49,345, the EV4 GT is pricier than an entry-level Golf GTI (£41,860) or indeed a Golf R (£46,930). However, being powered by batteries should make for much lower running costs than either – provided you have an EV charger installed at home. 

Kia also offers its famous seven year, 100,000-mile warranty, plus a long list of standard equipment. The fully loaded GT spec includes intelligent LED headlights, heated and ventilated front seats, 360-degree parking cameras, ambient interior lighting, an electric tailgate and an eight-speaker Harman Kardon sound system. The only option of note is ‘premium’ paint, such as the Blue Flame colour seen here (£650).

You can tell the GT apart from a regular EV4 by its beefier bumpers, gloss-black trim and neon green brake calipers, which are tucked inside 20-inch alloy wheels. Inside, there’s more neon green on the seatbelts and dashboard, along with alloy pedals and bucket seats trimmed in faux leather and suede. 

You want numbers? Zero to 62mph takes 5.6 seconds, top speed is 105mph and kerb weight is 2,060kg. The EV-specific stats are 81.4kWh (size of the lithium-ion battery), 128kW (maximum charging speed) 3.4 miles per kWh (energy consumption) and 313 miles (driving range in the official WLTP test).

The Kia GT story so far

Kia’s GT badge has been around since the bizarrely punctuated Pro_cee’d GT of 2013. However, apart from the flagship 585hp EV6 GT, the vehicles it was affixed to have been ‘warm’ rather than explicitly hot. They were all overshadowed by sister brand Hyundai’s more extroverted and exciting ‘N’ cars, too.

This is the first GT model developed from scratch by Manfred Harrer, Kia’s head of R&D since 2025, whose CV includes 14 years at Porsche. It slots into the range between the also-new EV3 GT crossover and EV5 GT SUV, but is the most overtly sporting of the trio. It’s expected to be the best-seller, too – although the EV4 GT exists more to boost Kia’s image than its bottom line. 

All of which brings us to a hotel car park somewhere north of Nice. The Mediterranean sun is shining, the EV4 GT is brimmed with fresh electrons and the route snakes across its sat-nav screen like tangled strands of spaghetti. Yep, we’ve all had worse days at work.

Fun for all the family

Kia’s futuristic ‘Opposites United’ design language works well on an SUV, but looks slab-sided and not particularly sporting here. Still, many will appreciate the GT’s ability to speak softly and carry a 292 horsepower stick. 

The advantage of that boxy body is plenty of passenger space, helped by the EV4’s ‘skateboard’ platform and flat floor. There’s room for three adults in the back, plus useful stowage in the deep door bins, centre armrest and seat-back pockets. There is no ‘frunk’ and the extra electric motor for the rear axle does rob some boot capacity, however. A total of 377 litres is 58 litres smaller than a standard EV4. 

Finding a good driving position is easy and the electric seats hug you in the right places. Kia’s in-car tech is also straightforward to use, with a 12.3-inch central touchscreen that syncs wirelessly with your smartphone via Apple CarPlay or Android Auto. The GT even has a data logger to measure your driving performance in real time. 

Inside the Kia EV4 GT

Despite the on-board telemetry and the presence of a new GT mode, Kia insists the hottest EV4 is ‘neither an out-and-out performance car, nor a track-day weapon’. The emphasis here, we’re told, is on ‘everyday usable power’ and a ‘familiar, comfortable character’. 

Accordingly, in the bustle of Nice’s morning rush-hour, the EV4 delivers relaxed, unobtrusive progress. It’s as easy to drive as any electric Kia, with light steering, a hushed soundtrack and decent all-round visibility. There’s also a full complement of electronic driver aids, such as blind-spot monitors and rear cross-traffic assist (to warn of approaching cars when you reverse out of a parking space).

In Normal mode, the Kia also has a commendably pliant ride, helped by a camera-based system that scans the road surface, preparing the dampers for what lies ahead. And today, as the Cote d’Azur soars majestically upwards into the Alpes-Maritimes, that means some of Europe’s very best driving roads. Route Napoleon, here we come.

A hotter way to go green

Push the neon green GT mode toggle on its steering wheel and the EV4 instantly feels energised. Its straight-line performance isn’t scorching by hot hatch standards – the latest Golf R is a second quicker to 62mph –  but the combination of all-wheel drive and an ever-ready 345lb ft of electric torque will slingshot you out of corners. On rural French D-roads, it gets you past dawdling motorhomes quickly and safely, too.

Kia has set up the GT to be primarily front-driven, in search of traditional hot hatchback handling balance (and more predictable behaviour at the limit, no doubt). Be abrupt with your right foot and all that can overwhelm the front wheels, leading to a scrabble for traction, but such instances are rare. For the most part, the EV4 feels calm and controlled, with limited body-roll and resolute grip from its EV-optimised rubber. 

Coming back to our Golf R comparison, the Kia has a similar ability to cover ground quickly, making light work of difficult roads. Its steering isn’t the last word in feedback and the regenerative brakes sometimes feel inconsistent. But it’s fun in a grown-up kind of way.

Like a video game made real

If you want something more involving/intriguing/immature (delete as appropriate), you can play with the Virtual Gear Shift. Previously seen in the Hyundai Ioniq 5 N, this simulates a six-speed manual transmission, accompanied by the snarl of a powerful petrol engine.

At first, the effect feels rather like playing a video game, but you soon forget the artifice and just enjoy the experience. Leave the VGS in automatic mode and it gives a convincing impression of a twin-clutch auto ’box. Alternatively, you can take control via paddles behind the steering wheel, which are otherwise used to adjust the level of brake energy recovery. The ‘redline’ is at 6,000rpm and you run out of revs at 7,100rpm, causing a lurch as the ‘engine’ bounces off its imaginary limiter. You can’t stall, but well-timed shifts are rewarded with swift, smooth progress.

As for the soundtrack, a member of Kia’s PR team likened it to the five-cylinder engine in an Audi RS3 and I can’t think of a better comparison. It’s quite different to the hot Hyundai, which has eight virtual gears and sounds more like a turbocharged four.  

Verdict: Kia EV4 GT

To paraphrase Mark Twain, reports of the hot hatchback’s death have been greatly exaggerated. Indeed, cars like the EV4 GT offer hope that an electric future doesn’t need to be dull. And if a part of their appeal lies in imitating a petrol car, so be it. If you don’t like the Virtual Gear Shift and five-cylinder fireworks, you can switch them off. 

Ultimately, the EV4 GT isn’t as entertaining as the benchmark Golf GTI, but it’s a quick and accomplished car that delivers on Kia’s goals to be comfortable and usable. If you’re in the market for a family EV and want more than just fuss-free transport and a long warranty, it’s well worth a look. 

Who knows, you might even find yourself tackling a great road just for the fun of it. If you’re in the area, may I recommend the Route Napoleon? Just allow yourself enough time to drive it twice.

• Tim Pitt writes for Motoring Research

On the internet, no one knows you’re a cat. But The Algorithm almost certainly knows if you’re a cat owner, and it will increasingly serve you content aimed at keeping your housebound feline entertained. Welcome to the YouTube phenomenon of Cat TV, a peculiar niche of video streaming whose primary audience (one has to assume) are crepuscular predators with names like Socks, Mr Biscuits and Santa Paws.

Like most internet phenomena, the origins of Cat TV are a mix of blind luck and ingenuity. One of the genre’s most popular content creators, who was at the forefront of the nascent industry some 10 years ago, is Cornwall-based amateur wildlife photographer Paul Dinning. His YouTube page describes an initial plan to film local bird species for the benefit of other nature lovers, which suddenly blew up when he experimented with the title Videos for Cats. Dinning’s account now has 832,000 subscribers and his most popular videos have amassed millions of views (his 10-minute piece about Cadgwith Cove has not yet broken the internet in quite the same way).

Jasper the half-Bengal juvenile cat is fixated

The content itself is unsurprising, for humans at least. I have a half-Bengal juvenile cat called Jasper who is fixated by these eight-hour long videos, filmed in static close-up, of cats, mice and squirrels nibbling at treats on feeder tables. As far as Jasper is concerned, these strange exercises are a high watermark of on-screen entertainment, second only to televised football, where occasional displays of metronomic passing in the mould of early-period Guardiola are known to activate his hunting instincts to such an extent he ends up body-slamming our flatscreen.

I’m less interested in the psychology of pets, however, than I am the motivation of the creators. A quick scroll of YouTube suggests this cottage industry may be more of a tower block. It turns out amateur enthusiasts like Dinning are the exception rather than the rule of Cat TV. If his early experiments in the form were a happy accident, it didn’t take long for the entrepreneurial twitchers of the internet to realise these recordings represent a simple way to capture a small slice of the attention economy.

Play Video

“These videos do well because YouTube ranks them on watch time,” says Adam Jones, the co-founder of social-first video production company Trendy Grandad. “If you watch 30 seconds, that feeds a bad sign into an algorithm. But if you watch five hours of it, that’s a great sign for the algorithm. It’s a good earner in terms of advertising revenue, and people do it to build up watch time and subscribers, which allows them to monetise other content later on. Essentially you’re farming watch time.”

‘Cat TV is more cut throat than you would ever imagine‘

This may explain why, after efforts to contact a large number of the accounts behind these videos, I received only one fairly cryptic response. “The world of Cat TV is probably more surprising and cut throat than you would ever imagine,” said an established creator in the field, who would speak only under the shadow of anonymity. “Due to this I am quite private about what I reveal about myself or my processes.” My follow-up questions went unanswered.

One positive we can draw from the Cat TV industry is that it does not yet appear to have been eaten up by AI: the majority of the videos are real films of critters. Content produced by channels with names such as Birder King and Cat Games have racked up millions of views, but search traffic is dominated by a relatively small number of players.

I came across half a dozen accounts struggling to succeed with this traffic fishing approach, with their videos only reaching the hundreds or low thousands of viewers, and in some cases far less. Zoë Glatt, a digital ethnographer at LSE, pointed out that while this type of content “may seem like an easy way to make a quick buck, research shows it is exceptionally hard to build a following and generate sustainable revenue as a content creator, especially in oversaturated content verticals with a low barrier to entry”.

Perhaps it’s only fitting that content designed for predators, whose natural bloodlust has yet to be bred out of them despite four thousand years of domestication, has given rise to a behind-the-scenes industry just as savage. Beneath the bright eyes and fur, there are always claws.

• Tom Duggins is a freelance journalist

On this day, the 1st October, in 1969, Concorde first showed off its real party trick, writes Eliot Wilson in the latest instalment of his on this day series

It was unusually windy around Toulouse on Wednesday 1 October 1969, the vent d’Autan blowing from the south-east. Its unpredictable gusts and changes in air pressure could drive people insane. Quand l’autan boufa, les bous d’Albi dancent, said the old Occitan proverb. When the Autan blows, the madmen of Albi dance.

At Toulouse-Blagnac Airport that morning, André Turcat hoped the winds would drop. Nearly 48, he had served with the Armée de l’Air, flying transport aircraft in Indochina before training as a test pilot. Turcat had overseen the experimental phase of the Nord 1500 Griffon ramjet-powered interceptor, and in 1959 he had broken the world speed record over 100km, at an average of 1,021 mph.

When the Griffon programme ended, Turcat left the air force for Sud Aviation, the state-owned aircraft manufacturer, just as it was about to embark on a joint venture with the British Aircraft Corporation (BAC). BAC and Sud Aviation had both been working on concepts for a supersonic passenger jet; Britain had applied to join the Common Market, while Sud Aviation needed modern large jet engines.

The result, in November 1962, was a formal international agreement, signed in London by minister of aviation Julian Amery and Geoffrey de Courcel, ambassador of the French Republic. The two companies would develop a supersonic commercial airliner: at a subsequent press conference, the project was first dubbed “Concorde”.

British pride had taken a knock. In the 1950s, its aeronautical industry had bristled with great names: Vickers-Armstrongs, de Havilland, English Electric, Avro, Hawker Siddeley, Gloster, Bristol, Fairey, Handley Page, Blackburn. And this rich array produced some of the best aircraft in the world.

The Gloster Meteor had been beaten to the punch as the first operational jet fighter by the Messerschmitt Me-262 by only days in 1944; the de Havilland Comet became the world’s first commercial jet airliner in 1952; and Britain’s nuclear strike force the “V-bombers” – the Vickers Valiant, the Avro Vulcan and the Handley Page Victor – were sophisticated and distinctive aircraft.

By the 1960s, it had all changed. Manufacturers were herded into the British Aircraft Corporation, its head office at the top of 100 Pall Mall. While it was partnering with Sud Aviation on Concorde, its hopes of ongoing military orders rested on the supersonic strike aircraft TSR-2. The aircraft would succumb to financial constraints and inter-Service rivalry, and was cancelled in 1965. Sir Sydney Camm, designer of the Hawker Hurricane, remarked mordantly: “All modern aircraft have four dimensions: span, length, height and politics. TSR-2 simply got the first three right.”

Concord or Concorde?

But there was Concorde. Or Concord? Shortly after the name was announced, President de Gaulle had vetoed the UK’s first application to join the Common Market, though his carefully worded speech never explicitly said “non”. Prime Minister Harold Macmillan, witty and cutting but secretly sensitive, pointedly dropped the “e” and preferred the standard English word ”concord”: agreement, harmony, union.

It bore more than a little irony: Macmillan had been minister resident in Algiers during the Second World War, where de Gaulle based the Free French headquarters for a time, and knew his prickly hauteur. In 1969, the minister of technology, Anthony Wedgwood Benn, announced in Toulouse he would return the name to “Concorde”, explaining “E stands for excellence, for England, for Europe and for the Entente Cordiale”. Macmillan was reliably funnier than Wedgie.

Concorde was like nothing aviation had seen before. Its narrow fuselage allowed for only four seats abreast, and a total capacity of between 92 and 128 passengers, but its delta wing and quartet of Rolls Royce/Snecma turbojets allowed it to cruise at twice the speed of sound for three-quarters of a transatlantic flight. Journey times fell by more than half.

The construction of two prototypes began in 1965. Sud Aviation built 001 at its huge plant at Blagnac Airport, while 002 was manufactured by the BAC Filton Division outside Bristol. The revolutionary and futuristic project caught the imagination, and within four years the consortium had received provisional orders for 74 aircraft from 16 airlines.

Breaking the sound barrier

Concorde 001 made its first flight from Toulouse on 1 March 1969 with Turcat at the controls. Legendary test pilot Brian Trubshaw flew 002 on her maiden flight on 9 April from Filton to RAF Fairford. He commented, “It was wizard – a cool, calm and collected operation”. But it was over Toulouse, today in 1969, that Turcat demonstrated Concorde’s real party trick.

For the first time, Concorde pushed effortlessly through the sound barrier, flying at around 690 mph for nine minutes without seeming out of breath. “All was perfectly calm,” Turcat told reporters afterwards over a glass of champagne. “The Concorde seems made for supersonic flight.” Deliveries of the aircraft would be in late 1973 or early 1974. The world of aviation had changed.

Or had it? Concorde would suffer a series of grievous wounds. The cost was spiralling, ending up six times as high as projected, £23bn by 1977. The energy crisis following the Yom Kippur War in 1973 highlighted Concorde’s thirst and the efficiency of slower, larger, wide-bodied aircraft.

But the coup de grâce was the very thing that made Concorde unique: in April 1973, concerned about pollution, take-off noise and the aircraft’s sonic boom, the Federal Aviation Administration banned supersonic flight over US territory. In anticipation, Air Canada, United Airlines, TWA, Pan Am, American Airlines, Eastern Airlines, Braniff and Continental Airlines had all cancelled their orders: 42 aircraft, more than half the total.

Concorde was not dead, but it would never change the face of flying. Only 20 would be built, and in the hands of British Airways and Air France they become an icon of luxury and privilege. BA’s Heathrow to JFK flight was promoted with the slogan “Arrive before you leave”: it took off at 10.30 am and it was wheels down in New York at 8.30 am local time. A classy trick, an astonishing achievement of engineering, but that was what Concorde would remain.

For its consulting practice, Accenture said it had booked six per cent more this quarter compared to the same period last year, hitting $9.3bn in revenue [£7bn].

AI ‘reckoning’ for consulting giants

Over the past 12 months, Accenture’s stock has plunged around 25 per cent, in part due to softer quarterly results, falling returns on invested capital and growing concerns around AI’s impact on the consultancy sector.

Analysts at Morningstar have downgraded firms like Accenture and Capgemini due to AI-fuelled uncertainty about their future sales pipelines.

“Professional services firms are in a tough position currently, with an AI disruption cloud hanging over their heads,” Michael Field, chief equity strategist at Morningstar, previously told City AM.

Hundreds of current and former shareholders in Home REIT have launched High Court proceedings against the scandal-hit property firm in a bid for compensation, accusing it of misleading investors and negligently misrepresenting its operations as a company.

Over 800 shareholders have hit the former London-listed social housing company with a claim for losses they allege were caused by misleading statements and omissions of key details about the company, its business model and property portfolio.

The proceedings have been brought against Home REIT and the the company’s directors. Its former investment adviser, Alvarium Home REIT Advisors, and former alternative fund manager, Alvarium Fund Managers, have also been named in the proceedings alongside others involved with the company.

The actions issued include statutory securities claims, which cover misleading reports or accounts, as well claims of deceit and negligent misrepresentation.

Sold a narrative that did not ‘reflect reality’

The investors allege the housing firm painted a misleading picture on the security of its rental income, tenant experience and valuation of its portfolio, all of which they say was “fundamental” in their decision to invest.

Home REIT raised more than £850m from investors in its first three years, telling shareholders their capital would be used to acquire accommodation for vulnerable and homeless people while also generating returns from rental income.

Investors were also informed that properties would be leased on long-term agreements to organisations providing accommodation to vulnerable people, allowing rental income to be supported by government-funded housing benefit.

Nate Barber, partner at Harcus Parker and lead lawyer for the claim, said: “Our case is that what investors were told did not reflect the reality. The allegations concern the security of Home REIT’s income, the financial strength of its tenants, its stated social impact, and the acquisition, use and valuation of its property portfolio.”

Twists and turns

Home REIT, which floated in 2020, has been rocked by a series of crises since the end of 2022, when a short seller, Viceroy Research, sounded the alarm on the make-up of its tenants in a damning report.

Previous reporting by City AM revealed in 2023 that a string of its biggest tenants had gone bust and it was repeatedly forced to offload chunks of its portfolio in attempts to raise cash and pay off debts.

Shares in the business were suspended in January 2023 after it failed to publish its annual accounts before a regulatory deadline. It was also found that some properties were marketed to students and holiday makers.

The UK’s top financial crime unit unveiled a major probe into its past management earlier this year, after identifying as much as £300m in suspected fraud and bribery. The Serious Fraud Office conducted a series of raids and arrests in January, searching properties in Maidenhead, Altrincham and London.

“What has happened since is extraordinary. Home REIT’s property portfolio has been sold, its four wholly owned subsidiaries are now in liquidation, and many investors have suffered significant losses,” Barber said.

“They are entitled to understand how that happened and, where they were misled, to seek compensation from those responsible.”

Home REIT said it “notes today’s announcement” and would not comment further. The firm added that an “announcement will be made at an appropriate time”.

  • Amuse bouches
  • Tuna sashimi

Yoh Yoshida:  Hi Victor, it’s so nice to see you again. It must be six months since we last caught up!

Victor Garvey:  Yeah, this will be your first time in MATER1A. You’re in for a treat. What brings you to London?

YY:  It’s a funny story – I have been playing a series of Shakespeare characters on the stage in Japan: Hamlet, Brutus and Richard III. After that I wanted to come here to pay tribute to the real Richard III, so I have been in Leicester to visit his grave at the cathedral.

VG:  It must be a really different experience to do Shakespeare in Japanese. I can’t imagine being able to keep the rhythm that Shakespeare originally intended in a language that takes longer to speak. If I say a sentence in English, it might be five words and take two seconds but the same sentence in Japanese is 12 words and takes six seconds. Japanese sentences are very descriptive, and they always have to have a place and a time – that’s just the way it works, right? YY:  Yes, it’s different. The translation I was working on was quite modern, similar to the way we speak now. Sometimes it can work in your favour though. Take the famous line: “A horse! A horse! VG:  So Yoshida-san, do you remember where we met?

YY:  Of course! I was in London for the Film Festival, promoting A Pale View of Hills, an adaptation of the novel by Kazuo Ishiguro. VG:  Yeah, the first time I visited Japan about 20 years ago I only had one tattoo but they still wouldn’t let me go in the onsen! Successfully refreshing a 250-year-old brand in Lloyds and a 350-year-old brand in Scottish Widows in the same year. Making them ready for the app and AI economies and everything that follows.

Uncertainty is the price of an interesting career. The certain jobs are rarely the interesting ones, and certainty is usually what a role feels like just before it becomes irrelevant.

“Stay in your lane.” Everything worthwhile I’ve done has happened in the gap between two lanes. Or an interesting never-trodden lane.

South-west London, deep in nappy valley.

Same place, usually on a bike. I commute on a Genesis, and when mine was stolen I tracked down the last one in the country at a hundred-year-old shop in Ipswich and went to collect it in person. Best day I’d had in months. And now I try to use it as often as I can.

Family, and Luna the dog, who is entirely non-negotiable. Which means the New Forest or Cornwall rather than anywhere requiring a passport and a kennel.

Britain’s AI minister has ordered changes to government guidance that urged civil servants to limit their use of AI, saying it failed to reflect ministers’ ambitions to ramp up adoption across Whitehall.

Kanishka Narayan said guidance published last week had now been updated after it advised government workers to use AI only when necessary, choose smaller models and keep prompts to a minimum to cut energy use and costs.

“Being environmentally conscious and keeping an eye on running costs is, of course, important – but so is encouraging AI adoption and scaling up its use across the public sector”, Narayan said on X.

“This advice has been updated and we are reviewing similar pages to reflect the fullness of our ambition for the UK”.

It comes just days after government guidance attracted attention for telling civil servants there was no need to thank AI chatbots, alongside recommendations to use lighter models such as Gemini Flash rather than Gemini Pro and GPT Instant instead of GPT Thinking.

The guidance said AI uses more energy and resources than conventional software and told staff to consider whether a spreadsheet or search engine could do the job instead.

Civil servants were also advised to keep prompts “short, clear and direct”, use as few prompts as possible and only turn to AI when needed,

The latest version instead puts greater emphasis on responsible use rather than discouraging unnecessary use.

It tells civil servants they remain responsible for their work when using AI and must check its output for inaccuracies, bias or unfairness.

Staff are also warned to protect sensitive information and use systems provided by their departments for government work.

“You are responsible for any content or decisions you make using AI”, the new advice says, telling officials to use their own judgement and be prepared to explain decisions made with the technology.

The change highlights the balancing act facing ministers as they push AI deeper into government while trying to control the risks and costs that come with it.

Whitehall’s AI push

The change in direction comes as the government looks to accelerate AI adoption across the public sector, an area that now falls directly within his ministerial responsibilities. Minister Narayan’s brief covers both the government’s AI strategy and public sector adoption.

Existing government guidance already encourages civil servants to explore how generative AI could improve their work, while warning them not to enter sensitive or personal information and to check outputs for misinformation and bias.

A government AI playbook published last year similarly set out ten principles for the use of the technology across Whitehall, covering how officials should select, buy and deploy AI safely.

But the push to accelerate adoption has come alongside concerns over how quickly AI is being introduced into public services and whether sufficient human oversight remains in place.

The government’s Responsible AI Advisory Panel discussed the need for effective coordination across Whitehall at its latest meeting in September as departments expand their use of the technology.

Narayan has nevertheless made expanding adoption a central part of his brief, arguing that Britain should develop and deploy advanced AI rather than allow the next technological shift to happen elsewhere.

Berenberg’s Investor Barometer, which polled 300 international investors managing a combined $1 trillion, found that 40 per cent pointed to policy decisions as the biggest risk to Britain’s economy, unchanged from the last poll despite a change of government.

The findings highlight a “continuing lack of confidence in the current administration’s long-term fiscal framework”, authors of the study wrote, despite the UK boasting the most ambitious deficit reduction path of any G7 economy.

“New Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s costly initial ambitions kept government policy at the top of the list of investor concerns,” Berenberg chief UK economist Andrew Wishart said. “Burnham and the Chancellor have since conceded that higher spending is the wrong choice when borrowing and the tax burden are already problematically high, which gives us some reassurance that they will avoid a major policy error.”

Uzbekistan’s national investment fund, Uznif, became the only IPO of note this year when it listed a 30 per cent stake on the London and Tashkent stock exchanges in May. London will be hit the hardest if Andy Burnham lowers the threshold for the ‘mansion tax’ to £1.5m – which only gets you a flat or an ordinary terraced house in many parts of the capital, says James Cleverly

Andy Burnham’s Family Homes Tax is yet another attack on London.

Last year, Rachel Reeves announced a surcharge of £2,500 to £7,500 a year on homes worth more than £2m. It was billed as a “mansion tax”, supposedly targeting “less than the top 1 per cent of properties”. Now, inevitably, Burnham is considering lowering the threshold to £1.5m. That would more than double the number of homes caught across England, to 271,000, and drag in nearly 62,000 more in London alone.

Outside of London, £1.5m might buy you something resembling a mansion. Inside London, it will often only get you a terraced house with a small garden.

Of the London homes sold between £1.5m and £2m last year, one in six were flats. Most of the rest were terraced houses. Nobody in Lewisham, where I was born, thinks that’s a mansion. Nor do they in Bexley and Bromley, where I served as an Assembly Member, or in Ealing, where I went to university and met my wife. 

You can see it on any property app. Three-bedroom terraces across London are on the market for around £1.5m. These are not mansions. They are ordinary family homes on ordinary streets, made expensive by decades of price rises.

The people who live in these homes are not multi-millionaires. They are teachers, nurses, electricians and retired workers who bought a house years ago, paid off the mortgage and raised a family. Hamptons found that 60 per cent of the homeowners who would pay the tax bought their home for less than £1.5m. House price inflation dragged them in. At £2,500 a year, the charge is over £200 a month on top of council tax, for a family whose only crime was buying a house in London a long time ago.

A double whammy for Londoners

Even Sadiq Khan has felt the pressure and now says he opposes it. He is right to. But the Mayor’s objection means little if his colleagues in Downing Street don’t listen.

When I was shadow housing secretary, I kept warning that Labour’s policies were driving up the cost of building. Higher energy costs. Higher material costs. Higher taxes on employing people. That is a double whammy for London. Young Londoners can’t afford a home, because it has been made harder and more expensive to build them. And those who have worked hard to buy their own home are now taxed for it. Labour is punishing both the people trying to get on the housing ladder and the people who climbed it.

It’s also unlikely any of the tax revenue raised from this hike would stay in London. Wandsworth, Kensington and Chelsea, Westminster and Richmond say their residents alone would pay over £270m a year, but not a penny would fund a local service. It goes straight to the Treasury. 

At the same time, Labour’s funding formula is stripping money out of those same boroughs, with Wandsworth alone losing £84m. That council’s finance chief called these plans “the most badly designed tax on properties since the one on windows, 330 years ago”. He has a point. Londoners pay more, London keeps less, and the money leaves the capital.

Andy Burnham does not understand London. He sees a city full of wealth and reaches for the cash. He does not see the families who bought a home, raised their children and want to stay put.

London needs a Mayor who will say no to this tax and back Londoners instead of treating them as a cash cow. That is the Mayor I intend to be.

James Cleverly is prospective Conservative candidate for Mayor of London
